docs.sectionTitle: Why bother with arrays at all?
docs.text: Every ML notebook you will ever write starts the same way: load a table, poke at it, clean it, plot it. This module makes those moves automatic. You already know Python lists. So why learn a second container that looks almost identical? Because of what happens when the data gets big. In the lecture, doubling two million numbers took 0.42 s with a Python loop and 0.015 s with NumPy — roughly 28 times faster. That gap is not NumPy being clever about arithmetic. It is where the loop runs . A Python for loop steps through boxed objects one at a time in the interpreter; NumPy hands the whole block to compiled C and gets out of the way. A Python loop is walking to office. NumPy is the metro. Same destination, one of them doesn't make you stop at every house.  The 28× matters for a different reason than impatience. A model fit is the same arithmetic repeated thousands of times. At Python-loop speed, cross-validating twenty hyperparameter settings is an overnight job; at NumPy speed it is a coffee break. Speed is what lets you try things , and trying things is how you actually learn which model fits. The scikit-learn models you will use for the rest of this course are NumPy underneath. When LinearRegression().fit(X, y) solves (XᵀX)⁻¹Xᵀy in one shot, that is NumPy calling the same LAPACK routines your university's physics department uses. You are not learning a toy — you are learning the interface to forty years of numerical computing.

A NumPy array is a grid of numbers of one type , stored as one contiguous block of memory. That single sentence explains almost everything that follows: the speed (no pointer-chasing), the strictness (no mixing strings and floats), and the shape rules. Creating arrays creating arrays import numpy as np

a     = np.array([1, 2, 3, 4, 5])      # from a list
zeros = np.zeros((2, 3))               # 2 rows x 3 cols of 0.0
ones  = np.ones((3, 3))
r     = np.arange(0, 10, 2)            # [0 2 4 6 8]  start, stop(excluded), step
lin   = np.linspace(0, 1, 5)           # [0. .25 .5 .75 1.] start, stop(included), num
m     = np.arange(1, 13).reshape(3, 4) # 3x4 grid of 1..12
print(m.shape, m.dtype) Read the last line out loud on every array you make: shape tells you the grid, dtype tells you whether your numbers are secretly strings. np.arange(0, 10, 2) stops before 10 → [0 2 4 6 8]. np.linspace(0, 1, 5) includes 1 → [0, .25, .5, .75, 1]. arange counts by a step , linspace counts by a number of points . a-RANGE = range with a step, end excluded. LIN-space = a LINE cut into N points, both ends kept. Which is why you reach for linspace when you want a smooth x-axis to plot a curve over: you ask for 200 points and you get exactly 200, both ends included. Indexing and slicing indexing and slicing arr1d = np.arange(10)
arr1d[3]        # single element -> 3
arr1d[2:7]      # slice -> [2 3 4 5 6]
arr1d[::-1]     # reversed

arr2d = np.arange(1, 13).reshape(3, 4)
arr2d[1, 2]     # row 1, col 2 -> 7
arr2d[:, 1]     # whole column 1 -> [2 6 10]
arr2d[0:2, 1:3] # sub-matrix rows 0-1, cols 1-2

safe = arr2d[0:2].copy()   # independent copy, edits won't leak back  Line by line: arr2d[1, 2] is one bracket with a comma inside, not arr2d[1][2] . Both happen to work, but the comma form is the one NumPy is built around and the only one that generalises to slices on both axes. A bare colon means "everything along this axis", so arr2d[:, 1] reads as "every row, column 1". Slices are views , not copies. b = a[0:2]; b[0] = 99 also changes a . When you want an independent piece, write a[0:2].copy() . This is the single most common source of "my data changed and I don't know why" in a notebook. Element-wise maths and broadcasting + - * / ** work slot by slot. A single number "broadcasts" across every slot, so x + 100 adds 100 everywhere. Two arrays must either have the same shape, or shapes NumPy can stretch to match — a (3, 4) array and a (4,) array combine fine, because the (4,) is reused for each of the three rows. A * B is element-wise. A @ B is matrix multiplication. Mixing them up gives a valid-looking but wrong answer, with no error — which is far worse than a crash. If a result looks plausible but your accuracy is strange, check your stars and ats first. Aggregation across an axis axis= is where most beginners stall, and it has exactly one rule. The axis you name is the axis that disappears. axis=0 squashes the rows away, so you get one answer per column. axis=1 squashes the columns away, one answer per row. Say it to yourself before every call and you will never get it backwards again. interactive lab axis Pick an operation and an axis, then hover an answer to see exactly which cells were squashed into it.

docs.sectionTitle: When to use it, and what goes wrong
docs.text: Reach for NumPy when Reach for something else when You have numbers of one type and want maths on all of them Your data has named columns and mixed types — that is Pandas You need speed: fitting, simulating, image or signal work You need to append repeatedly in a loop — a Python list is better, convert once at the end A library asks for an array of shape (n_samples, n_features) You are holding text, categories or anything heterogeneous  Three failure modes are worth recognising on sight: Silent dtype promotion. Put one string in an integer array and the whole thing becomes <U21 strings. Your arithmetic then concatenates instead of adding. print(a.dtype) is the two-second check. Shape mismatch that doesn't error. Broadcasting is helpful right up until it quietly stretches something you meant to keep separate. If a result has a shape you didn't expect, stop and print the shapes of both operands. Views leaking edits. The .copy() trap above. It bites hardest when you slice a training set out of a bigger array and then normalise it in place. ISLP Ch 2 The ISLP lab sections for chapter 2 cover exactly this ground — array creation, indexing and the shape conventions — with the same (n_samples, n_features) discipline that scikit-learn enforces from Module 3 onwards.

The arithmetic above is not abstract. Here it is on the course's own employee table — 240 rows, with deliberate gaps in salary , which is what makes it a realistic first dataset rather than a tidy one. dataset employee the same moves, on the course data import numpy as np
import pandas as pd

df = pd.read_csv("employee_dataset.csv")
salary = df["salary"].to_numpy()        # a (240,) float array, NaN where missing

salary.shape        # (240,)
np.isnan(salary).sum()                  # how many gaps NumPy sees

# NaN is contagious: one gap poisons the whole aggregate.
salary.mean()                           # nan
np.nanmean(salary)                      # the mean of the values we do have

# Element-wise maths, no loop in sight
raise_pct = (salary * 1.07) - salary    # what a 7% rise would cost per head
np.nansum(raise_pct).round(2)           # total cost of the rise Run this and `salary.mean()` prints `nan`. That is NumPy being honest: it will not invent a number for a gap. Handling the gap is a decision you make, in the next chapter.

Open a notebook next to employee_dataset.csv and work these without looking anything up. The goal is for the syntax to stop costing you attention. Build np.arange(1, 13).reshape(3, 4) . Before running anything, write down what np.sum(m, axis=0) and np.sum(m, axis=1) will be. Then check. Success: you predicted both shapes and both sets of values. Pull years_experience into an array. Compute its mean, std, min and max with NumPy, then again with the Pandas .describe() you will meet next chapter. Success: the numbers agree — except std, and you can say why (ddof). Take a = np.arange(10) , slice b = a[2:5] , set b[0] = 99 , and print a . Success: you can explain the result to someone else in one sentence. Normalise the salary array to the 0–1 range using only broadcasting: (x - nanmin) / (nanmax - nanmin) . Success: the result's min is 0.0 and max is 1.0. Stretch goals Time the 28× yourself: double two million numbers with a list comprehension and with an array, using %%timeit in Jupyter. See how close you get to the lecture's 0.42 s versus 0.015 s. Write np.sum(m, axis=1) using only m.shape and a Python loop, then convince yourself the vectorised version is doing the same thing — just not in Python.

A Python loop is walking to office. NumPy is the metro. a-RANGE = range with a step, end excluded. LIN-space = a LINE cut into N points, both ends kept. The axis you name is the axis that disappears. Slices are windows, not photocopies. Star multiplies slot by slot. At multiplies matrices. Matrix m is 2×3. What does np.sum(m, axis=1) return? Two numbers, one per row. axis=1 removes the column axis, so each row collapses to a single sum. For [[1,2,3],[4,5,6]] that is [6, 15] . Why is NumPy faster than a Python list for the same arithmetic? The elements are one dtype in one contiguous block, so the loop runs in compiled C rather than stepping through boxed Python objects in the interpreter. The lecture measured 0.42 s versus 0.015 s on two million doublings. Is a[0:2] a copy? No — a view. Editing it edits the original. Use .copy() when you need an independent piece. What is the difference between A * B and A @ B ? * is element-wise, slot by slot. @ is matrix multiplication, rows against columns. Confusing them produces a wrong answer with no error.

A DataFrame is a NumPy grid with row labels and column names attached. Same maths, but the labels travel with the data. That sounds like a convenience. It is actually the difference between code you can read in six months and code you cannot. Compare X[:, 4] with df["salary"] . Both fetch the same numbers. Only one of them survives a colleague inserting a column. Every data role runs on this. "Average salary per department", "tickets closed per agent", "revenue per region" — every dashboard KPI you have ever seen is a groupby plus an aggregation underneath, and somebody wrote it in about four lines. There is a second, quieter reason. Real data is dirty . It has gaps, wrong types, duplicates and surprises. NumPy will happily compute a mean over a column of strings-pretending-to-be-numbers and give you nonsense. Pandas gives you the tools to find out before you model anything — which is the entire job of the first hour on any dataset.

The first five calls on any dataset Call Answers df.head() / df.tail() What do the rows look like? df.shape How many rows and columns? (no brackets — it's an attribute) df.dtypes Is every column the type I expect? (numbers stored as text is a classic) df.describe() count, mean, std, min, quartiles, max for numeric columns df.info() types + non-null counts + memory: spots missing values fast  "Hey, Show Data In Detail" head → shape → dtypes → info → describe. Run them in this order on every new file. The order matters: you want to see the rows before you trust any summary of them. Why this order, concretely. head() tells you whether the file even parsed — a shifted header or a stray index column shows up immediately. shape tells you whether you loaded all of it. dtypes catches the number-stored-as-text problem while it is still cheap to fix. info() then shows non-null counts, which is where missing values first become visible. Only then does describe() mean anything, because by that point you know what it is describing. Selecting rows and columns selection import pandas as pd
df = pd.read_csv("employee_dataset.csv")

df["department"]                         # one column -> Series
df[["department", "salary"]]             # several columns -> DataFrame

df.loc[0:4, ["department", "salary"]]    # by LABEL, end included (5 rows)
df.iloc[0:5, 1:4]                        # by POSITION, end excluded

df[df["salary"] > 90000]                 # boolean mask
df[(df["department"] == "Sales") & (df["salary"] > 60000)]
df[~df["remote"].eq("Yes")]              # ~ means NOT
df.query("department == 'Sales' and salary > 60000")   # same, readable  Two details in there are worth slowing down for. One bracket or two. df["salary"] gives a Series (1D); df[["salary"]] gives a DataFrame (2D). This looks like trivia until Module 3, where scikit-learn demands X as 2D (n_samples, n_features) and y as 1D (n_samples,) . The double bracket is how you produce the 2D one. It is the single most common beginner error in the whole course. Masks are arrays, not conditions. df["salary"] > 90000 evaluates to a Series of True/False, one per row. Putting that inside df[...] keeps the True rows. Nothing clever is happening — you are indexing with a boolean array, exactly as in NumPy. loc = Labels. iloc = Integer location. loc slices include the end label (0:4 gives 5 rows). iloc slices exclude the end, like normal Python. On a default index the two look identical, which is exactly why the difference catches people out later. Combine conditions with & , | , ~ and wrap each condition in brackets. Python's and / or raise "truth value of a Series is ambiguous" — they want a single True or False, and you handed them 240 of them. Missing values finding and filling gaps df.isna().sum()                     # missing count per column
df.isna().mean().round(3) * 100     # missing % per column
df.dropna()                         # drop rows with ANY missing value
df.dropna(subset=["salary"])        # only rows missing salary
df = df.fillna({
    "salary": df["salary"].median(),                     # skewed -> median
    "performance_score": df["performance_score"].mean()  # symmetric -> mean
})  Which strategy to pick: drop rows when very few are missing and they look random; fill with the median for skewed numbers (salary), the mean for symmetric ones, and the mode for categories. From Week 1 onward, compute those fill values on the training split only . A median is a statistic; if you compute it over all the rows, your test rows have influenced how the training rows were cleaned. That is leakage, and it quietly inflates every score you report afterwards. This becomes a graded point in Module 3. Group, sort, count split, apply, combine df.groupby("department")["salary"].mean()

df.groupby("department").agg(
    avg_salary=("salary", "mean"),
    headcount=("employee_id", "count"),
    max_exp=("years_experience", "max"),
).sort_values("avg_salary", ascending=False)

df.sort_values("salary", ascending=False).head(10)
df["department"].value_counts()                  # counts
df["department"].value_counts(normalize=True)    # proportions The named-aggregation form in the middle is the one worth memorising: it produces readable column names instead of a MultiIndex you then have to flatten. groupby is a laundry SAC: Split the clothes by colour, Apply the wash, Combine them back in the basket. Split–Apply–Combine is the actual name of the pattern, and it is the same idea as SQL's GROUP BY and a spreadsheet pivot table.

docs.sectionTitle: Live: gaps and fences on the real column
docs.text: Before filling a gap you have to know the shape of the column you are filling it in. Salary in this dataset is right-skewed with a long upper tail, which is exactly the case where the mean and the median disagree — and the case where the median is the honest choice. interactive lab iqr

SettingWithCopyWarning. You sliced a DataFrame and then assigned into the slice. Pandas cannot tell whether you meant to edit the original. Fix it by slicing with .loc in one statement, or by taking an explicit .copy() first — the same view-versus-copy issue as NumPy slices. Numbers stored as text. df.dtypes says object where you expected float64 . One stray space or currency symbol does it. pd.to_numeric(col, errors="coerce") converts what it can and turns the rest into NaN, which you can then count. Chained indexing. df["a"][0] = 5 may or may not stick. df.loc[0, "a"] = 5 always does. Dropping too much. df.dropna() with no arguments removes a row if any column is missing. On a wide table that can delete most of your data. Always check .shape before and after. ISLP Ch 2 ISLP's chapter 2 lab walks the same loading-and-inspecting routine on its own datasets, and its treatment of the index and of boolean selection is worth reading alongside this chapter.

dataset employee the first hour on employee_dataset.csv df = pd.read_csv("employee_dataset.csv")

df.shape                # (240, 8)
df.dtypes               # salary is float64 because of the NaNs
df.isna().sum()         # salary and performance_score have gaps

# Fill salary with the median of its own department, not the global median:
# a Sales median and an Engineering median are different numbers.
df["salary"] = df.groupby("department")["salary"].transform(
    lambda s: s.fillna(s.median())
)

df.groupby("department").agg(
    avg_salary=("salary", "mean"),
    headcount=("employee_id", "count"),
).sort_values("avg_salary", ascending=False) `transform` is the one to know here: it returns a result the same length as the original, so it can be assigned straight back into the column. Notice what the per-department fill buys you. The global median ignores that departments pay differently, so filling an Engineering gap with the company-wide median pulls that row towards Support. Grouping first keeps the structure you already know is there.

Run the five calls in order on employee_dataset.csv . Success: you can state the shape, name every column whose dtype surprised you, and give the missing count per column from memory. Select Engineering staff earning above 100k, using a mask and again with .query() . Success: both return the same number of rows. Count missing values per column, then fill salary with the median per department (the transform above). Success: df.isna().sum() is zero for salary and the departmental means moved only slightly. Produce mean salary and headcount per department, sorted by mean salary descending. Success: one table, readable column names, no MultiIndex to flatten. Stretch goals Does remote work relate to satisfaction? Group by remote and compare satisfaction_score . Then ask yourself whether a difference in means is enough to claim anything — you will have the tools to answer that properly in Module 1. Rebuild your departmental summary with pivot_table instead of groupby().agg() and decide which one you would rather read next year.

"Hey, Show Data In Detail" — head, shape, dtypes, info, describe. loc = Labels (end included). iloc = Integer location (end excluded). Pandas logic speaks & | ~, and every condition needs its own brackets. groupby is a laundry SAC: Split, Apply, Combine. One bracket gives a Series, two give a DataFrame — and sklearn wants the DataFrame. df.loc[0:4] and df.iloc[0:4] on a default index return how many rows? Five and four. loc slices by label and includes the end label; iloc slices by position and excludes it, like normal Python. Why does df[df.a > 1 and df.b fail? Python's and needs a single True or False and was handed a whole Series. Use (df.a > 1) & (df.b < 2) , each condition in its own brackets. Median or mean to fill a missing salary, and why? Median. Salary is right-skewed — a few very high values drag the mean up, so the mean is not representative of a typical row. Why must fill values be computed on the training split only? A median is a statistic learnt from data. Computing it over all rows lets test rows influence how training rows were cleaned, which is data leakage and makes the reported score optimistic.

docs.chapterTitle: Plotting: pick the chart by the question
docs.text: You can summarise a column to four numbers and still have no idea what it looks like. Anscombe's quartet is the famous demonstration: four datasets with identical means, identical variances, identical correlation and identical regression lines, which look nothing like each other once drawn. One is a clean line, one is a curve, one is a line plus a single outlier, one is a vertical stack. Every model in this course assumes something about shape. A linear model assumes a straight-line relation. A z-score outlier check assumes a bell. PCA assumes the spread is along straight directions. Plotting is how you check the assumption before you spend an afternoon on a model that was never going to fit. The practical version of this: you will be asked "why did the model do badly?" far more often than "how does the algorithm work?". Nine times out of ten the answer is visible in a histogram or a scatter plot you could have drawn in the first ten minutes.

docs.chapterTitle: Plotting: pick the chart by the question
docs.text:
Stop choosing charts by taste. Choose them by the question you are asking, which has exactly one sensible answer each time. Question Chart Call What does one column look like? Histogram plt.hist(df.salary.dropna(), bins=20) How do two columns move together? Scatter plt.scatter(df.years_experience, df.salary) How does a number differ across groups? Box plot sns.boxplot(data=df, x="department", y="salary") How do many columns relate at once? Heatmap sns.heatmap(df[num].corr(), annot=True, cmap="coolwarm") Several views side by side? Subplots fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2)  1 column → hist. 2 columns → scatter. Groups → box. Grid of everything → heatmap. Count the columns in your question first. That alone narrows it to one or two options every time. matplotlib or seaborn? They are not competitors. Seaborn is built on matplotlib and knows about DataFrames: you pass data=df, x="department", y="salary" and it handles the grouping, the colours and the legend. Matplotlib is the layer underneath, where you control every element by hand. Practical rule: reach for seaborn when the chart involves a category (box plots, bar plots by group, pair plots, heatmaps) and matplotlib when you are drawing raw numbers (histograms, scatters, lines, anything you are building up piece by piece). Then use matplotlib to adjust whatever seaborn produced, because the result is a matplotlib axes either way. the Week 0 figure import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import seaborn as sns

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(15, 4))
axes[0].hist(df["salary"].dropna(), bins=20)
axes[0].set_title("Salary distribution")
axes[1].scatter(df["years_experience"], df["salary"], alpha=0.6)
axes[1].set_xlabel("Years of experience"); axes[1].set_ylabel("Salary")
sns.boxplot(data=df, x="department", y="salary", ax=axes[2])
axes[2].tick_params(axis="x", rotation=45)
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()

num = df.select_dtypes("number").columns
sns.heatmap(df[num].corr(), annot=True, cmap="coolwarm", vmin=-1, vmax=1)
plt.title("Correlation heatmap"); plt.show() Three details that matter: `.dropna()` because hist cannot handle NaN, `alpha=0.6` because overlapping points hide density, and `vmin/vmax` on the heatmap so the colour scale means the same thing in every figure you ever draw. With subplots you call methods on each axes[i] , and the names change: plt.title() becomes ax.set_title() , plt.xlabel() becomes ax.set_xlabel() . The rule is simple once you see it — the pyplot functions are verbs, the axes versions are set_ plus the noun. Why the two interfaces exist at all: plt.hist(...) draws on whichever axes is "current", which is fine for one chart and unmanageable for six. fig, axes = plt.subplots(...) hands you the objects explicitly, so there is never any doubt about which panel you are drawing on. Use the explicit form as soon as you have more than one panel. Reading a box plot The box plot is the densest of the five and the one most often misread. The box is Q1 to Q3 — the middle half of the data. The line inside it is the median , not the mean. The whiskers reach to the furthest point still inside the 1.5 × IQR fence, and anything beyond is drawn as an individual dot. So a box plot is really a five-number summary plus a flag for outliers, which is why it answers "how does this differ across groups" so well: you get centre, spread and tails for every group at once.

docs.chapterTitle: Plotting: pick the chart by the question
docs.sectionTitle: Live: the fence behind the whiskers
docs.text: Those dots past the whiskers are not a judgement, they are an arithmetic rule with a multiplier in it. Drag the multiplier and watch the same column gain and lose "outliers" without a single value changing. interactive lab iqr

docs.chapterTitle: Plotting: pick the chart by the question
docs.text: Too few or too many bins. A histogram with 5 bins hides the shape; one with 200 bins on 240 rows shows noise. Start at 20 and move once you have looked. Overplotting. Thousands of scatter points become a solid blob. Fix with alpha , a smaller marker ( s=5 ), or a hexbin. The study guide's Q3 does exactly this: 20,640 housing points plotted with s=5, alpha=0.3 . Truncated or inconsistent colour scales. A correlation heatmap without vmin=-1, vmax=1 rescales itself to whatever is in this matrix, so the same colour means different things in two figures side by side. Forgetting the NaNs. plt.hist raises on missing values; seaborn silently drops them. Either way, know how many went missing before you read anything off the chart. Unlabelled axes. Costs marks in the assessment and costs you time in six months. The rubric checks for it. Assignment-1 awards marks for the plot itself and for its labelling. Q3 wants a 2D scatter of input against target; Q5 wants that same scatter with the fitted line drawn over it in a distinguishable colour. Title, x-label and y-label on every figure. ISLP Ch 2 ISLP's chapter 2 lab covers the same plotting vocabulary, and its figures are a good model for what a publishable version of each of these charts looks like.

docs.chapterTitle: Plotting: pick the chart by the question
docs.sectionTitle: On the real data: the six lecture steps
docs.text:
240 employees, with deliberate missing salaries and performance scores. These are the six steps from the Week 0 lab, in order. dataset employee Load and inspect: shape, dtypes, missing counts Select: Engineering staff earning above 100k, only name-like columns Aggregate: mean salary and headcount per department Histogram of salary Scatter of experience vs salary Heatmap of numeric correlations Solution code for all six steps m0 practice solution import pandas as pd, numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt, seaborn as sns

# 1. load and inspect
df = pd.read_csv("employee_dataset.csv")
print(df.shape)
print(df.dtypes)
print(df.isna().sum())

# 2. select
eng = df[(df["department"] == "Engineering") & (df["salary"] > 100000)]
print(eng[["employee_id", "department", "salary"]])

# 3. aggregate
summary = df.groupby("department").agg(
    avg_salary=("salary", "mean"),
    headcount=("employee_id", "count"),
).sort_values("avg_salary", ascending=False)
print(summary)

# 4-6. the three charts
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(15, 4))
axes[0].hist(df["salary"].dropna(), bins=20)
axes[0].set_title("Salary distribution")
axes[0].set_xlabel("Salary"); axes[0].set_ylabel("Employees")

axes[1].scatter(df["years_experience"], df["salary"], alpha=0.6)
axes[1].set_title("Experience vs salary")
axes[1].set_xlabel("Years of experience"); axes[1].set_ylabel("Salary")

sns.boxplot(data=df, x="department", y="salary", ax=axes[2])
axes[2].set_title("Salary by department")
axes[2].tick_params(axis="x", rotation=45)
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()

num = df.select_dtypes("number").columns
sns.heatmap(df[num].corr(), annot=True, cmap="coolwarm", vmin=-1, vmax=1)
plt.title("Correlation heatmap"); plt.show()  What to actually read off the output: the salary histogram has a long right tail (so median, not mean, for filling gaps); the experience-versus-salary scatter rises but with real spread (so a line will fit, imperfectly); and the heatmap shows experience and salary as the strongest pair, which is the relationship Module 4 will model properly.

docs.chapterTitle: Plotting: pick the chart by the question
docs.text: Work the six steps above without looking at the solution. Success: every figure has a title and both axis labels, and you can say one sentence about what each chart told you. Box plot of salary by department. Success: you can name the department with the most outliers and say whether you would treat them as errors or as real high earners. Pick any two numeric columns and predict the sign of their correlation before computing it. Success: you were right about the sign on at least four of five pairs. Redraw the salary histogram with 5, 20 and 100 bins. Success: you can argue for one of them. Stretch goals Build the same three-panel figure for students_survey.csv , which you will meet properly in Module 1. The code should barely change — that is the point of the lookup table. Recreate Anscombe's quartet with sns.load_dataset("anscombe") and confirm for yourself that four identical summaries can describe four different pictures.

docs.chapterTitle: Plotting: pick the chart by the question
docs.text: 1 column → hist. 2 columns → scatter. Groups → box. Grid of everything → heatmap. Seaborn for categories, matplotlib for raw numbers — and seaborn returns a matplotlib axes anyway. On an axes object, pyplot verbs become set_ plus the noun. The line in a box is the median; the whiskers stop at the 1.5 × IQR fence. Always pin a correlation heatmap to vmin=-1, vmax=1. Which chart answers "how does salary differ across departments"? A box plot — one box per department gives centre, spread and outliers for every group in a single figure. With subplots, why does axes[0].title("x") fail? Axes objects use set_ methods: set_title , set_xlabel , set_ylabel . The bare verbs belong to the pyplot interface. Your scatter plot is a solid blob. What do you change? Reduce marker size and add transparency — s=5, alpha=0.3 — or switch to a hexbin. The study guide's housing scatter uses exactly that for 20,640 points. Why plot before modelling at all? Every model assumes a shape. Anscombe's quartet shows four datasets with identical summary statistics and completely different shapes — only the plot distinguishes them.

docs.chapterTitle: Where is the middle, and how spread out?
docs.sectionTitle: Why the average can be a lie
docs.text: Statistics describes the data you have. Probability reasons about data you haven't seen yet. Every ML model is a mix of the two. Nine people at a Kolkata tea stall earn ₹30k a month each. A billionaire sits down. The mean income at the stall jumps to crores; the median barely moves. That is why salary reports quote the median. This is not a trick question about tea stalls. It is the reason you will be asked, in Module 3, to fill a missing salary with a median rather than a mean, and the reason a single mislabelled sensor reading can wreck a model trained on squared error. "Where is the middle" and "how spread out" are the two questions you answer about every column before you do anything else. Get them wrong and every later decision inherits the error.

docs.chapterTitle: Where is the middle, and how spread out?
docs.text:
Three kinds of middle Measure What it is Outliers? Use when Mean Sum ÷ count Very sensitive Symmetric data (heights, exam scores) Median Middle value after sorting Robust Skewed data (income, house prices, wait times) Mode Most frequent value Robust Categories (most common department)  Lecture data [4, 8, 15, 16, 23, 42, 8, 8, 15] : mean = 15.4, median = 15, mode = 8. Notice how close mean and median are here — and then notice that 42 is the only thing pulling them apart. Remove it and the mean drops to 11.1 while the median moves to 15 → 15. That asymmetry of response is robustness. The Mean is mean to outliers. The Median stays in the middle of the road. The Mode is the most popular kid.  Two kinds of spread Variance and standard deviation variance σ² = average of (x − mean)²
std σ = √variance   ← same units as the data Variance squares distances so negatives don't cancel positives. Standard deviation undoes the square so you can say "salaries vary by about ₹12k" instead of "₹144M²". It is worth being precise about why we square rather than taking absolute values. Squaring is differentiable everywhere, which matters enormously from Module 4 onward: mean squared error has a clean gradient, and that gradient is what gradient descent follows. Absolute error does not, at zero. The choice of square is partly about outliers and largely about calculus. np.std(x) divides by n (population). df["col"].std() divides by n − 1 (sample). On small data they differ noticeably. Use np.std(x, ddof=1) to match Pandas. If your NumPy and Pandas standard deviations disagree, this is always why. Percentiles, IQR and the outlier fence The p-th percentile has p% of values below it. Q1 = 25th, Q3 = 75th. IQR = Q3 − Q1 is the spread of the middle half, and unlike the range it ignores extreme values entirely — which is exactly what you want when the extremes are what you are trying to find. IQR outlier rule (used in every course notebook) lower fence = Q1 − 1.5 × IQR
upper fence = Q3 + 1.5 × IQR
anything outside a fence → flag as an outlier "One and a half boxes out, and you're out." The box in a box plot is the IQR. Step 1.5 box-lengths beyond either edge: that's the fence. Where does 1.5 come from? It is a convention, not a theorem. For normally distributed data the fences sit at roughly ±2.7σ, so about 0.7% of genuine values fall outside them. Tukey picked it because it flags few enough points to be worth looking at and enough to be useful. Knowing it is a convention is the point: it means the number of "outliers" in your data is partly a choice you made. interactive lab iqr

docs.chapterTitle: Where is the middle, and how spread out?
docs.text: Quoting a mean on skewed data. If mean and median disagree by much, say which one you are using and why. A mean salary that no employee earns is not a useful summary. Comparing standard deviations across units. ₹12k of salary spread and 12 marks of exam spread are not comparable. Divide by the mean to get a coefficient of variation, or standardise. Treating the fence as truth. The fence flags candidates for inspection, not errors. In fraud detection the flagged points are the entire product. Population versus sample std. The ddof trap above — it will also explain a mismatch between your answer and the solution notebook. Don't delete flagged points on reflex. First ask whether it is an error in the raw data (a typo, a broken sensor — fix or drop) or a rare-but-real event (keep, and sometimes it is the whole point). Module 3 makes this a formal step in the pipeline. ISLP Ch 2 ISLP chapter 2 sets up exactly this vocabulary before any model appears, and its treatment of variance as the thing bias–variance decomposition is built from is worth reading before Module 5.

docs.chapterTitle: Where is the middle, and how spread out?
docs.text:
dataset students the lecture's own numbers, then the real survey import numpy as np, pandas as pd
from scipy import stats

data = np.array([4, 8, 15, 16, 23, 42, 8, 8, 15])
np.mean(data), np.median(data), stats.mode(data, keepdims=False).mode
np.var(data), np.std(data), np.std(data, ddof=1)     # population vs sample

q1, q3 = np.percentile(data, [25, 75])
iqr = q3 - q1
lower, upper = q1 - 1.5 * iqr, q3 + 1.5 * iqr
outliers = data[(data < lower) | (data > upper)]     # -> [42]

df = pd.read_csv("students_survey.csv")
df[["study_hours_per_week", "exam_score"]].describe() On the lecture array the fence flags exactly one value, 42 — the same number that was dragging the mean up. That is the fence doing its job. Run .describe() on the survey and read the gap between mean and 50% for each column. Where they are close, the column is roughly symmetric and a mean is honest. Where they diverge, you have found skew without drawing anything.

docs.chapterTitle: Where is the middle, and how spread out?
docs.text: Compute mean, median, std and IQR for every numeric column in students_survey.csv . Success: one tidy table, and you can name the most skewed column from the mean-versus-median gap alone. Reproduce the lecture array's outlier detection by hand: percentiles, IQR, both fences, the flagged values. Success: you get [42] and your numbers match np.percentile . For exam_score , count how many points the 1.5 fence flags and how many the 3.0 fence flags. Success: you can say which you would use for a grading appeal and which for a data-quality check. Show the ddof trap: print np.std(x) and df['x'].std() for a 9-element column. Success: you can state the ratio between them before running it. Stretch goals Add one extreme value to exam_score and watch what happens to mean, median, std and IQR. Rank the four by how much they moved — that ranking is what "robust" means. Write your own quantile(sorted, q) with linear interpolation and check it against np.percentile on several columns.

docs.chapterTitle: Where is the middle, and how spread out?
docs.text: The Mean is mean to outliers. The Median stays in the middle of the road. Variance squares so negatives don't cancel; std un-squares so the units make sense. One and a half boxes out, and you're out. np.std divides by n, pandas .std() divides by n − 1. 1.5 is a convention, so the outlier count is partly your choice. Mean or median for a typical income, and why? Median. Income is right-skewed; a few very large values drag the mean up, so the mean describes nobody. Why does variance square the deviations? So negative and positive deviations do not cancel — and, more importantly for later, because the squared loss is differentiable everywhere, which is what gradient descent needs. Where do the IQR fences sit, and is 1.5 principled? Q1 − 1.5·IQR and Q3 + 1.5·IQR. The 1.5 is a convention, not a theorem; for normal data it corresponds to roughly ±2.7σ, flagging about 0.7% of genuine values. np.std(x) and df['x'].std() disagree. Why? Different denominators: NumPy uses n (population) and pandas uses n − 1 (sample). Pass ddof=1 to NumPy to match.

docs.sectionTitle: Why a curve instead of a number
docs.text: A summary statistic tells you about the data you have. A distribution tells you what to expect from data you have not seen — which is the only thing that matters when you deploy a model. Concretely: "the exam mean is 70" does not tell you whether a 92 is remarkable. "Scores are roughly normal with μ = 70 and σ = 10" tells you 92 is 2.2σ out, which happens about 1.4% of the time. That second statement is actionable; the first is not. A call centre where each call converts with p = 0.3: "how many sales out of the next 10 calls?" is Binomial(10, 0.3). The most likely answer is 3, but 1 or 5 happen often enough that a manager shouldn't panic about a single shift. Knowing the distribution is the difference between managing and reacting.

A distribution maps every possible outcome to its probability. Discrete ones (Bernoulli, Binomial) give a probability per outcome via a PMF. Continuous ones (Normal) give a density via a PDF; the area under the curve is the probability. pMf → Marbles you can count. pDf → Density you measure as area. This is why P(X = 70.000…) is zero for a continuous variable: a single point has no width, so no area. You can only ask for the probability of a range. Normal (Gaussian) Bell-shaped, symmetric around μ, width set by σ. Heights, measurement errors, exam scores, and — crucially — sums of many small random effects. That last one is the central limit theorem, and it is why the normal keeps appearing in places with no obvious reason to be bell-shaped: anything that is the sum of many small independent contributions tends towards it. interactive lab normal  "68, 95, 99.7 — one, two, three steps to heaven." Within 1σ: 68%. Within 2σ: 95%. Within 3σ: 99.7%. A value beyond 3σ is a 3-in-1000 event; that is the logic behind z-score outlier checks. The rule holds whatever μ and σ you pick, which is what makes it worth memorising. Shift the centre, stretch the width — the fractions do not move. That invariance is the whole content of the z-score: z = (x − μ)/σ converts any normal variable into the standard one, so a single table of areas serves every normal distribution there has ever been. Bernoulli and Binomial Bernoulli(p) : one yes/no trial (one coin flip, one email spam or not). Binomial(n, p) : count the yeses in n independent trials. A Bernoulli is just a Binomial with n = 1. Binomial PMF P(k successes in n trials) = C(n, k) · p^k · (1 − p)^(n − k)
mean = n·p        variance = n·p·(1 − p)
Binomial(10, 0.3): mean 3, variance 2.1, std ≈ 1.45 The three pieces read left to right: C(n, k) counts how many orderings give k successes, p^k is the probability of the successes, (1−p)^(n−k) the probability of the failures. The independence assumption is doing all the work in that multiplication — if calls in a shift are correlated (a bad script, a broken line), Binomial is the wrong model. scipy.stats answers "what should this distribution look like?" ( .pdf() , .pmf() , .cdf() ). np.random answers "give me fake data that looks like this" ( np.random.normal(70, 10, 1000) ). Theory versus simulation — you will use both, and confusing them is how people end up plotting a histogram where they meant a curve. theory and simulation side by side from scipy import stats
import numpy as np, matplotlib.pyplot as plt

x = np.linspace(-4, 4, 400)
plt.plot(x, stats.norm.pdf(x, loc=0, scale=1)); plt.title("Standard normal"); plt.show()

stats.norm.cdf(1) - stats.norm.cdf(-1)     # 0.6827 -> the 68% rule

np.random.binomial(n=1, p=0.3)             # Bernoulli: one trial
k = np.arange(0, 11)
plt.bar(k, stats.binom.pmf(k, n=10, p=0.3)); plt.title("Binomial(10, 0.3)"); plt.show()

sample = np.random.normal(loc=70, scale=10, size=1000)   # fake exam scores
plt.hist(sample, bins=30); plt.show() Line 7 is the 68% rule computed rather than recited: the CDF at +1 minus the CDF at −1 is 0.6827.

Assuming normality because it is convenient. Income, wait times, counts and anything bounded below at zero are usually not normal. Plot it; a histogram with a long right tail is a refusal. Using a z-score fence on skewed data. If the distribution is not symmetric, ±3σ is not the 0.3% boundary you think it is. Use the IQR fence instead. Forgetting independence. Binomial requires independent trials with constant p. Ten calls handled by the same tired agent are neither. Reading a PDF value as a probability. A density can exceed 1. Only areas are probabilities. ISLP Ch 4 ISLP chapter 4 builds classification on top of these distributions — the Bayes classifier it opens with, and LDA later, both assume a distributional form for each class. Reading it after this chapter makes the assumption visible.

dataset students Treat exam_score as the candidate normal variable and passed as the Bernoulli one. Those two columns let you exercise both halves of this chapter against 300 real rows: fit μ and σ to the scores and check the 68-95-99.7 fractions empirically, then count the pass rate and ask whether Binomial would describe a random sample of 10 students. checking the rule against the survey df = pd.read_csv("students_survey.csv")
scores = df["exam_score"]
mu, sigma = scores.mean(), scores.std(ddof=1)

for k in (1, 2, 3):
    inside = scores.between(mu - k * sigma, mu + k * sigma).mean()
    print(k, round(inside * 100, 1), "% vs theory", round(
        (stats.norm.cdf(k) - stats.norm.cdf(-k)) * 100, 1))

# the Bernoulli half
p = (df["passed"] == "Yes").mean()
print("pass rate", round(p, 3), "| Binomial(10, p) mean", round(10 * p, 2)) The empirical fractions will not land exactly on 68.3 / 95.4 / 99.7 — 300 rows is a small sample, and that gap is itself worth reasoning about.

Plot exam_score and study_hours_per_week and guess each one's distribution shape before computing anything. Success: you can justify "roughly normal" or "not normal" from the picture. Run the 68-95-99.7 check above. Success: you can say how far the empirical fractions are from theory and whether 300 rows explains the gap. Draw the Binomial(10, 0.3) PMF as a bar chart and mark its mean. Success: the mean lands at 3 and you can read off P(exactly 5). Simulate 1,000 exam scores with np.random.normal(70, 10, 1000) and overlay the theoretical PDF on the histogram. Success: both are on the same axes with the histogram density-normalised. Stretch goals Demonstrate the central limit theorem: draw 10,000 samples of 30 values each from a deliberately non-normal distribution (uniform, or exponential), histogram the 10,000 sample means, and watch a bell appear. Compare the IQR fence and the ±3σ fence on study_hours_per_week . Where they disagree, decide which you trust and say why.

pMf → Marbles you can count. pDf → Density you measure as area. 68, 95, 99.7 — one, two, three steps to heaven, whatever μ and σ are. A Bernoulli is a Binomial with n = 1. scipy.stats is theory; np.random is simulation. Only areas are probabilities — a density can exceed 1. What fraction of a normal distribution lies within 2σ of the mean? About 95% — 95.45% exactly. Within 1σ it is 68.3% and within 3σ 99.7%, and those fractions do not depend on μ or σ. Difference between a PMF and a PDF? A PMF gives the probability of each discrete outcome and the values are probabilities. A PDF gives a density for a continuous variable; probability is the area under it, so a single point has probability zero. When does Binomial stop being the right model? When the trials are not independent or p is not constant across them — correlated calls, a changing script, a learning agent. Why does the normal keep showing up? The central limit theorem: anything that is the sum of many small independent contributions tends towards a normal distribution, whatever the individual contributions look like.

P(flagged | at risk) and P(at risk | flagged) are different numbers, and confusing them is one of the most expensive mistakes in applied statistics. A screening test can be 90% accurate at detecting a condition and still be wrong nine times out of ten when it fires — if the condition is rare enough. That is not a paradox and it is not a flaw in the test. It is arithmetic, and Bayes' theorem is the arithmetic. Bank fraud alerts, cancer screening, spam filters (Naive Bayes is literally this formula applied word by word), and incident triage that flags "probable outage": all of them fight the low-base-rate problem. Every one of them has a team arguing about where to put the threshold.

Joint, marginal, conditional Build a two-way count table with pd.crosstab , divide by the grand total, and you have joint probabilities. Sum across a row or column and you get the marginals — they live in the table's margins, which is where the name comes from. Conditional probability P(A | B) = P(A and B) / P(B)
"Zoom into B's world. What fraction of it is A?" That one-line gloss is worth more than the formula. Conditioning is restriction : you throw away every row where B did not happen, and then ask what fraction of what remains has A. The denominator P(B) is just renormalising so the surviving rows add to 1. Independence A and B are independent  ⇔  P(A | B) = P(A)
Knowing B happened changes nothing about A. Bayes' theorem Both conditionals share the same joint: P(A|B)·P(B) = P(A and B) = P(B|A)·P(A). Divide by P(B) and you have the theorem. That is the entire derivation — there is nothing else in it. Bayes P(A | B) = P(B | A) × P(A) / P(B)
posterior = likelihood × prior / evidence
evidence P(B) = P(B|A)P(A) + P(B|not A)P(not A) Word Symbol Plain meaning Prior P(A) What you believed before the evidence Likelihood P(B | A) How likely the evidence is if A were true Evidence P(B) How likely the evidence is overall Posterior P(A | B) Updated belief after seeing the evidence  "Post = Like × Prior ÷ Evidence" Read it as: new belief = (how well the evidence fits) × (old belief), rescaled so everything adds to 1. The three lecture examples Coin: prior 0.5 this person flips; P(heads | them) = 0.7, P(heads | other) = 0.5. Seeing heads, P(them) = 0.35 / 0.60 = 0.583 . Study group: P(group C | passed) via Bayes matches the direct table lookup exactly. Bayes is not magic, it is the table read backwards. Screening quiz: 2% at-risk, 90% detection, 15% false alarms. Flagged → only 10.9% are truly at-risk. interactive lab bayes  When the thing is rare, a positive test is mostly false alarms. Always imagine 1,000 people. 20 are at-risk, 18 get flagged. 980 are fine, 147 still get flagged. 18 out of 165 ≈ 11%. That counting version is the one to reach for under pressure. Nobody computes 0.9 × 0.02 / (0.9 × 0.02 + 0.15 × 0.98) in their head reliably, but almost anyone can count 18 out of 165. The formula and the headcount are the same calculation; the headcount is the one you can check. the table, both ways counts = pd.crosstab(df["study_group"], df["passed"])
joint  = counts / counts.values.sum()          # P(group and passed)
p_group  = joint.sum(axis=1)                   # marginal P(group)
p_passed = joint.sum(axis=0)                   # marginal P(passed)

p_yes_given_c = joint.loc["C", "Yes"] / p_group["C"]
independent = np.isclose(p_passed["Yes"], p_yes_given_c)

# Bayes: P(C | Yes) two ways
bayes  = p_yes_given_c * p_group["C"] / p_passed["Yes"]
direct = joint.loc["C", "Yes"] / p_passed["Yes"]
print(round(bayes, 4), round(direct, 4))       # identical The last line is the point of the exercise: Bayes and the direct lookup print the same number, because they are the same division written two ways.

The prosecutor's fallacy. "The test is 90% accurate, so there is a 90% chance you have it" swaps the conditional. The 90% is P(flagged | at risk). What the patient wants is P(at risk | flagged), and without the prior you cannot get there. Forgetting the evidence term. P(B) is not 1 and it is not the false-alarm rate — it is the total probability of being flagged, from both groups. Half the arithmetic errors live here. Assuming independence to make the maths work. Naive Bayes does exactly this on purpose and says so in its name. Doing it silently is different. A prior pulled from nowhere. The posterior is only as good as the prior. In the screening example, the entire conclusion rests on "2% at risk" being right. Rounding mid-calculation. With small probabilities, rounding the numerator and denominator separately can move the answer by several percentage points. ISLP Ch 4 ISLP chapter 4 opens with the Bayes classifier — the theoretically optimal one — and everything after it is an attempt to approximate it from data. Logistic regression in Module 4 is one such attempt.

dataset students study_group (A–D) crossed with passed (Yes/No) is a genuine 4 × 2 table, which is enough to exercise every term in the formula. Compute P(passed | group C) by restriction, then recover P(group C | passed) by Bayes, and check it against the direct lookup. When the two agree to the last decimal you have understood the theorem rather than memorised it. Then test independence: is P(passed | group C) equal to P(passed)? If the groups genuinely differ, it is not — and the size of the gap is the size of the group effect.

Build the joint table of study_group × passed and both sets of marginals. Success: the joint table sums to 1.0 and each marginal sums to 1.0. Compute P(passed | group C) by restriction. Success: you got it from the table without a formula. Get P(group C | passed) by Bayes and by direct lookup. Success: identical to four decimal places. Reproduce the screening quiz: 2% at-risk, 90% detection, 15% false alarms. Success: you get 10.9% and you can show the 1,000-person headcount that proves it. Stretch goals Find the prevalence at which the screening test's posterior crosses 50% — the point where a positive result becomes more likely true than false. Then argue about whether that is the right threshold for a screening programme. Test independence for every pair of categorical columns in the survey, and rank the pairs by how far P(A|B) sits from P(A).

Conditioning is restriction: zoom into B's world, then ask what fraction is A. Post = Like × Prior ÷ Evidence. When the thing is rare, a positive test is mostly false alarms. Bayes is not magic — it is the joint table read backwards. Always sanity-check with 1,000 imaginary people. A test detects 90% of cases and false-alarms on 15% of healthy people. The condition affects 2%. Someone is flagged — what is the chance they have it? About 10.9%. Of 1,000 people, 20 are at risk and 18 are flagged; 980 are healthy and 147 are flagged. 18 / 165 ≈ 10.9%. What is the evidence term P(B) made of? The total probability of the evidence from every source: P(B|A)P(A) + P(B|¬A)P(¬A). It is not the false-alarm rate alone. What does independence mean in one line? P(A | B) = P(A) — knowing B happened changes nothing about A. Why is the prior so important here? The posterior is the likelihood reweighted by the prior. With a rare condition the prior is tiny, so even a good likelihood cannot lift the posterior far — which is exactly the rare-disease result.

docs.sectionTitle: Why r is the most over-read number in statistics
docs.text: Correlation is the number people quote when they want to sound quantitative, and it is the number most often quoted wrongly. It measures one specific thing — how well a straight line describes the relation between two columns — and says nothing at all about cause, about curves, or about whether the relationship holds outside the range you measured. You will still draw a correlation heatmap on every dataset in this course, because it is the fastest way to find the pairs worth looking at. The discipline is in what you do next: look at the scatter plot before you believe the number. In Module 3's pipeline you will drop features whose absolute correlation exceeds 0.9, because two columns saying the same thing give a linear model two ways to express one idea and make its coefficients unstable. That is correlation used correctly: as a redundancy detector, not a causality detector.

Pearson r Spearman ρ Measures Straight-line relationship Monotonic (always up or always down) relationship Computed on Raw values Ranks of the values Outliers Sensitive Robust Pandas .corr() (default) .corr(method="spearman")  Pearson, written out r = Σ(xᵢ − x̄)(yᵢ − ȳ) / √[ Σ(xᵢ − x̄)² · Σ(yᵢ − ȳ)² ]
  = covariance(x, y) / (σₓ · σᵧ)
range −1 … +1 The numerator is the covariance you met in the spread chapter: it is large and positive when x and y are above their means together. The denominator divides out both columns' own spread, which is what makes r unitless and comparable across pairs. Correlation is covariance with the units cancelled. Pearson is a perfectionist about straight lines. Spearman only checks that the staircase keeps going up.  Range is −1 to +1. +1 perfect rise together, −1 one rises as the other falls, 0 no linear relation (a perfect U-shape can still have r ≈ 0). That parenthetical is the whole lesson: r = 0 means "no straight line fits", not "no relationship". When to reach for Spearman: when the relation is clearly monotonic but bent (diminishing returns — study hours against marks flattens out at the top), when either column is ordinal rather than interval (a 1–10 confidence rating is a rank, not a measurement), or when a couple of extreme values are dominating Pearson. Correlation never tells you why. Ice-cream sales and drownings both rise in summer: heat is the hidden confounder . Attendance and exam score correlate, but motivation may drive both. both coefficients, then the heatmap r   = df["study_hours_per_week"].corr(df["exam_score"])                  # Pearson
rho = df["exam_score"].corr(df["confidence_rating"], method="spearman")  # Spearman

num = df.select_dtypes("number").drop(columns="student_id")
sns.heatmap(num.corr(), annot=True, cmap="coolwarm", vmin=-1, vmax=1); plt.show() Dropping student_id matters: an ID is a number but not a measurement, and leaving it in puts a meaningless row and column in every heatmap you draw.

There is a geometric reading of Pearson worth having: once both columns are centred, r is the cosine of the angle between them as vectors. Perfectly aligned → cos = 1. Perpendicular → cos = 0 → uncorrelated. Opposed → −1. Module 2 builds this properly, but the lab is here because seeing it once makes r stop feeling arbitrary. interactive lab vectors

Reading causation into it. The classic. Always ask what third thing could drive both. Trusting r on a curve. A strong U-shape gives r ≈ 0. Plot it. Trusting r with outliers. One extreme pair can create or destroy a correlation on its own. Compare against Spearman as a cheap robustness check — a big gap between them means something is dragging Pearson. Restriction of range. Correlating height and basketball ability among professional players gives nearly zero, because everybody is tall. The relationship is real; your sample removed it. Correlating an ID or an index. Meaningless, and it clutters the heatmap. ISLP Ch 3 ISLP chapter 3 covers multicollinearity properly — what happens to a regression's coefficients and standard errors when two predictors are strongly correlated. That is the theory behind the |r| > 0.9 feature-dropping rule you will apply in Module 3.

dataset students The survey's interesting pair is confidence_rating against exam_score . Confidence is a 1–10 self-rating — an ordinal scale with no guarantee that the gap from 7 to 8 equals the gap from 2 to 3. That is precisely the case Spearman was built for, and comparing the two coefficients on this pair is the practice task the professor set. Pearson vs Spearman, side by side pairs = [("study_hours_per_week", "exam_score"),
         ("confidence_rating", "exam_score"),
         ("attendance_pct", "exam_score"),
         ("sleep_hours_per_night", "exam_score")]

for a, b in pairs:
    r   = df[a].corr(df[b])
    rho = df[a].corr(df[b], method="spearman")
    print(f"{a:24s} r={r:+.3f}  rho={rho:+.3f}  gap={abs(r - rho):.3f}") Sort by that last column. The pair with the biggest gap is the one where Pearson is being pulled by outliers or by a bend, and the one whose scatter plot you should open first.

Draw the full correlation heatmap for the survey, with student_id dropped and the scale pinned to −1…+1. Success: you can name the strongest positive pair and the strongest negative pair. Compute Pearson and Spearman for confidence_rating against exam_score . Success: you can argue which one to report, in one sentence, and it mentions the word ordinal . Pick the pair with the largest Pearson–Spearman gap and plot it. Success: you can point at what is causing the gap. For the strongest correlated pair, write down one plausible confounder. Success: your confounder is a third variable, not a restatement of either column. Stretch goals Construct a column with r ≈ 0 against exam_score that is nonetheless perfectly predictable from it (hint: a U-shape). Then show Spearman is also near zero, and say why neither coefficient caught it. Add one extreme outlier to the survey and recompute every Pearson coefficient. Rank the pairs by how far they moved — that is your sensitivity audit.

Pearson is a perfectionist about straight lines. Spearman only checks the staircase keeps going up. Correlation is covariance with the units cancelled — and, geometrically, the cosine between two centred columns. r = 0 means no straight line fits, not no relationship. A large Pearson–Spearman gap is a cheap outlier or curvature detector. Always pin the heatmap to vmin=−1, vmax=+1, and drop the ID columns first. A dataset has r ≈ 0 between two columns. Can they still be related? Yes. r measures linear association only; a perfect U-shape or any symmetric non-monotonic relation gives r near zero. When would you report Spearman instead of Pearson? When the relation is monotonic but bent, when a column is ordinal rather than interval (a 1–10 rating), or when a few extreme values are dominating Pearson. Ice-cream sales correlate with drownings. What is going on? A confounder — heat drives both. Correlation never identifies the direction or the existence of a causal path. Why drop features with |r| > 0.9 before fitting a linear model? Multicollinearity: two columns carrying the same information give the model two ways to express one effect, which makes the individual coefficients unstable and uninterpretable.

docs.chapterTitle: What a vector is, and the three operations
docs.text: Everything in this module is built from two things you already do: multiply two numbers, then add the results. Draw it in 2D, trust it in 1,536D. Running example, and it is worth holding onto for the whole module: a support desk counts two words in each ticket, "password" and "billing". Those counts are the ticket's vector. Ticket Text gist Vector [password, billing] T1 reset link never arrives, password page times out [2, 0] T2 billing page shows one charge, statement shows two [0, 2] T3 password change failed, billing page rejects address [2, 2]  Nothing has been added to the tickets. The vector is the tickets, counted. Every embedding you will ever use is this move with a cleverer counter and more slots — and once a thing is a vector you can measure how close two of them are, which is the entire mechanism behind semantic search, recommendation and retrieval.

docs.chapterTitle: What a vector is, and the three operations
docs.text:
One object, three readings List [2, 2]: order gives each slot its meaning. Use this view when computing . Point : an address on graph paper. Use it when plotting . Arrow from the origin: direction (what it's about) + length (how strongly). Use it when adding and comparing angles . L-P-A: List to compute, Point to plot, Arrow to add. They are the same numbers. Switching reading is free, and picking the right one makes most linear-algebra questions obvious. The dimension is just the number of slots. Two here; a typical sentence embedding has 1,536. Nobody can picture 1,536D and nobody needs to: every formula works slot by slot. This is the single most useful thing to internalise in this module — you reason in 2D and the arithmetic carries over unchanged. Adding, scaling, subtracting Slot by slot m + a = [4, 1] + [1, 3] = [5, 4]        (tip to tail)
2 × [2, 1] = [4, 2]                    (same direction, longer)
w − ℓ = [6, 2] − [2, 3] = [4, −1]      (the trip from ℓ to w) The parentheses are the geometry. Addition is tip-to-tail: walk along the first arrow, then along the second. Scaling stretches without turning. Subtraction gives you the arrow from one point to another, which is why error is always target minus prediction and never the other way round. Physics: a plane flying east at 500 km/h in a 60 km/h north wind actually travels 504 km/h, about 7° off course. Recommender: profile [1, 4] (years of camping gear) + query [4, 1] (just typed "cookware") = blend [5, 5]. Scale the query by 2 to say "trust the search box more". Normalising: divide a vector by its own length and it becomes length 1. [2,1] and [6,3] both land on [0.89, 0.45]: same subject, size removed. Drift: December [4,1] − June [1,4] = [3, −3]: tickets up 3, logins down 3. Churn monitors watch this difference arrow, not either endpoint. Operation Ask yourself Where it lives in AI Add "Both influences acting together?" Residual connections, token + position embeddings, profile + query blending Subtract "How do I get from b to a?" Error = target − prediction, task vectors, erasing a concept Scale "Same direction, different strength?" Learning rate × gradient, guidance strength, attention ÷ √d  That right-hand column is not decoration. When you meet w ← w − η·∇L in Module 4, it is scale-then-subtract. When you meet attention in a transformer, the ÷ √d is a scale. Learning the three operations well here means those later formulas have no new ideas in them. the three operations in NumPy import numpy as np
t, p = np.array([4, 3]), np.array([2, 4])

t + p, 2 * t, t - p        # add, scale, subtract

# normalise: same direction, length 1
unit = t / np.linalg.norm(t)
np.linalg.norm(unit)       # 1.0

# the same numbers, 1536 slots instead of 2 — nothing in the code changes
big_a, big_b = np.random.randn(1536), np.random.randn(1536)
(big_a + big_b).shape      # (1536,) The last two lines are the point: the code that works on two slots works on 1,536 with no edit. That is why the 2D picture is enough.

docs.chapterTitle: What a vector is, and the three operations
docs.text: Adding vectors whose slots mean different things. [years of service, salary] + [age, bonus] is arithmetic on nonsense. The slot order is the meaning; two vectors must share it. Forgetting that length carries information. Normalising throws away magnitude. For "same subject, different length" that is exactly right; for "how strongly" it destroys the signal. Subtracting in the wrong order. target − prediction and prediction − target differ by a sign, and that sign is the direction gradient descent will step in. Mixing shapes. In NumPy a (3,) and a (3, 1) look alike and broadcast into a (3, 3) . Print the shape. ISLP Ch 2 ISLP's notation section sets the convention this course follows — observations in rows, features in columns — which is what makes a row of the data matrix the vector for one example.

docs.chapterTitle: What a vector is, and the three operations
docs.text:
dataset cancer Each of the 569 tumours in the Wisconsin data is a 30-slot vector. That is already far past anything you can picture, and it does not matter: the row is a list when you compute, and in Module 4 a linear model will take its dot product with a weight vector of the same 30 slots. one tumour as a vector import pandas as pd, numpy as np

df = pd.read_csv("breast_cancer.csv").drop(columns=["Unnamed: 0", "id"], errors="ignore")
X = df.drop(columns="diagnosis").to_numpy()
X.shape                      # (569, 30) -> 569 vectors of 30 slots

a, b = X[0], X[1]            # two tumours
diff = a - b                 # the arrow from tumour 1 to tumour 0
np.abs(diff).argmax()        # which feature separates them most (by raw size)

# ...but raw size is misleading here: area_mean runs in the thousands and
# smoothness_mean in the hundredths. Scaling is coming in Module 3 for exactly this.
df.describe().loc[["min", "max"]].T.head(8) Run the last line and look at the ranges. `area_mean` spans ~140 to ~2500 while `smoothness_mean` spans ~0.05 to ~0.16. Any distance computed on these raw columns is a measure of area and nothing else.

docs.chapterTitle: What a vector is, and the three operations
docs.text: Build the three support tickets as arrays and compute T1 + T2, 2·T3, T3 − T1. Success: you can say in words what each result means about the tickets. Normalise [2, 1] and [6, 3] and confirm both give [0.89, 0.45]. Success: you can explain what information the normalisation threw away and when you would want that. Load the breast-cancer matrix and print its shape. Success: you get (569, 30) and can name what each axis is. Compute the difference vector between a malignant and a benign row, and find the feature with the largest absolute gap. Success: you noticed the answer is dominated by whichever column has the biggest units, and you can say why that is a problem. Stretch goals Compute the mean malignant vector and the mean benign vector, then the arrow between them. Which slots have the largest components? Keep the answer — Module 4's logistic weights should agree with it. Repeat the difference exercise after dividing every column by its own standard deviation, and watch the "most important feature" answer change completely.

docs.chapterTitle: What a vector is, and the three operations
docs.text: L-P-A: List to compute, Point to plot, Arrow to add. Dimension is just the number of slots; every formula works slot by slot. Add = both influences together. Subtract = the trip from b to a. Scale = same direction, different strength. Normalising keeps the subject and throws away the size. Slot order is the meaning — two vectors must share it to be added. Give the AI use of each of the three operations. Add: residual connections and token + position embeddings. Subtract: error = target − prediction, and task vectors. Scale: learning rate × gradient, and attention divided by √d. What does normalising a vector do, and what does it cost? Divides by its own length so it becomes length 1, keeping direction and discarding magnitude. That is right when size is noise (document length) and wrong when size is signal (intensity). Why is a 1,536-dimensional embedding not harder than a 2D vector? Every operation is defined slot by slot, so the arithmetic is identical. Only the visualisation fails, and the visualisation was never load-bearing.

docs.chapterTitle: The dot product and cosine similarity
docs.sectionTitle: Why one number matters this much
docs.text: The dot product is the single most load-bearing operation in machine learning. A linear model's prediction is a dot product. A logistic regression's score is a dot product. An SVM's decision is a dot product with each support vector. Attention in a transformer is a dot product between a query and a key. If you understand this one operation properly, a surprising amount of the rest is bookkeeping. It has two readings, and the trick is that they are the same number. Read one way it is a weighted score : each feature times how much it matters, added up. Read the other way it is length times length times the cosine of the angle . The first reading is why models use it; the second is why search engines use it.

docs.chapterTitle: The dot product and cosine similarity
docs.text:
Recipe: pair up, multiply, add t = [4, 3],  p = [2, 4]
t · p = 4×2 + 3×4 = 8 + 12 = 20      ← a single number "Zip, multiply, sum." It's a weighted score: each feature × how much it matters, added up. Days waiting 4×2 + tier 3×5 + "urgent" words 2×1 = priority 25. Sign: positive = leaning the same way, zero = perpendicular (nothing shared), negative = pulling against each other. Picture two kids pushing a wagon — same direction and the effort adds, opposite and it cancels, at right angles and neither helps the other. Length comes free: v · v = 4² + 3² = 25, so |v| = √25 = 5. That's Pythagoras, unchanged from school. A vector dotted with itself is its squared length, which is also why the L2 norm and the dot product are never far apart in a formula. Two readings, one number t · p = |t| × |p| × cos θ
20 = 5 × 4.47 × 0.89 Cosine similarity A three-line ticket [2,1] and a three-paragraph ticket [6,3] about the same issue point the same way, but distance says they're far apart. Throw away length, keep the angle: Cosine similarity cos θ = (a · b) / (|a| × |b|)      range −1 … +1
[4,3] vs [2,4]: 20 / (5 × 4.47) = 0.89  (≈ 27°) The division is doing exactly one thing: cancelling both lengths out of the dot product, so what is left is purely about direction. That is the whole difference between "dot product" and "cosine similarity" — one is a score that grows with size, the other is a score that ignores it. interactive lab vectors  This is semantic search and the retrieval step of RAG. The ticket "I can't log in, my password expired" becomes 1,536 numbers; so does every help article. Cosine 0.91 → "Resetting an expired password" is sent; 0.64 → offered second; 0.12 and 0.03 → discarded. Where you put the cut-off is a product decision, not maths. dot product, length, cosine import numpy as np
t, p = np.array([4, 3]), np.array([2, 4])

t @ p                      # dot product -> 20   (same as np.dot(t, p))
np.linalg.norm(t)          # L2 length -> 5.0
cos = t @ p / (np.linalg.norm(t) * np.linalg.norm(p))   # 0.894

from sklearn.metrics.pairwise import cosine_similarity
cosine_similarity([t], [p])          # same, for whole matrices of vectors `cosine_similarity` takes matrices, so it gives you every pairwise score in one call — which is how a vector database answers a query against a million documents.

docs.chapterTitle: The dot product and cosine similarity
docs.text: Comparing dot products across differently-sized vectors. A long document scores higher against everything simply because it is long. If size is not part of what you mean by similar, use cosine. Using cosine when magnitude is the signal. Two users with identical taste but wildly different activity levels have cosine 1.0. If you are predicting spend, that is the wrong answer. Unscaled features. A dot product on [salary in rupees, years of service] is a measure of salary. This is the same trap as distance, and the fix is the same: standardise first. Reading cos θ = 0 as "opposite". Zero is perpendicular — nothing shared. Opposite is −1. a * b in NumPy is element-wise and returns a vector ; a @ b is the dot product and returns a number . Both run without error on two vectors of the same length, so the only sign you used the wrong one is a shape you did not expect. ISLP Ch 2 ISLP introduces the matrix-vector notation this chapter's arithmetic underlies; from chapter 3 onwards every fitted value ŷᵢ in the book is a dot product of a row of X with the coefficient vector.

docs.chapterTitle: The dot product and cosine similarity
docs.text:
dataset cancer Here is the retrieval idea run against real rows: pick one tumour, score it against all 568 others by cosine, and look at whether its nearest neighbours share its diagnosis. If they do, the data is separable and the linear classifier in Module 3 will work. If they do not, no amount of model tuning will save it. nearest neighbours by cosine, on scaled features import pandas as pd, numpy as np
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler
from sklearn.metrics.pairwise import cosine_similarity

df = pd.read_csv("breast_cancer.csv").drop(columns=["Unnamed: 0", "id"], errors="ignore")
y = (df["diagnosis"] == "M").to_numpy()
X = StandardScaler().fit_transform(df.drop(columns="diagnosis"))   # scale FIRST

sims = cosine_similarity(X[:1], X)[0]      # one tumour vs all 569
order = np.argsort(-sims)[1:11]            # top 10, skipping itself

print("query is malignant:", y[0])
print("neighbours malignant:", y[order].sum(), "of 10")
print("similarity range:", sims[order].min().round(3), "-", sims[order].max().round(3)) Scaling before the cosine is not optional here. Run it on the raw columns and `area_mean` alone decides every neighbour, because it is three orders of magnitude bigger than `smoothness_mean`.

docs.chapterTitle: The dot product and cosine similarity
docs.text: Compute t · p, |t|, |p| and cos θ for the lecture's [4,3] and [2,4] by hand, then check with NumPy. Success: 20, 5, 4.47, 0.89 and you can show the two readings agree. Build a priority score: days waiting × 2 + tier × 5 + urgent words × 1, as a dot product with a weight vector. Success: you get 25 for [4, 3, 2] and can say which weight dominates. Run the nearest-neighbour code above, with and without StandardScaler . Success: you can state how many of the top 10 share the query's diagnosis in each case. Take two vectors with cosine 1.0 but very different lengths. Success: you can name a task where that is the right answer and one where it is wrong. Stretch goals Build a tiny RAG retriever: write five short help-article titles, hand-count two keyword features for each, and rank them against a query ticket by cosine. Then pick a cut-off and defend it. Show that cosine similarity on mean-centred columns is exactly the Pearson correlation from Module 1. Doing this once makes both concepts permanent.

docs.chapterTitle: The dot product and cosine similarity
docs.text: Zip, multiply, sum — and the answer is one number, not a vector. Positive = same way, zero = perpendicular, negative = opposing. v · v is the squared length, so Pythagoras comes free. Cosine is the dot product with both lengths divided out. Scale features before any dot product or distance, or the biggest-unit column decides everything. Give both readings of the dot product. A weighted score — each feature times its weight, summed. And |a||b|cos θ — length times length times the cosine of the angle between them. They are the same number. Why does retrieval use cosine rather than distance? Because document length should not count as dissimilarity. Cosine divides both magnitudes out, so a short and a long document about the same thing score alike. Two vectors have cos θ = 0. What does that mean? They are perpendicular — they share nothing. Opposite would be −1. What does a * b give you in NumPy, versus a @ b ? * is element-wise and returns a vector; @ is the dot product and returns a scalar. Both run without error, so the wrong one fails silently.

docs.sectionTitle: Why there is more than one kind of distance
docs.text: "How far apart are these two things" has more than one correct answer, and the choice is not arbitrary — it changes what your model does. This chapter looks like a detour into geometry. It is actually the setup for one of the most practically useful facts in Module 4: Ridge shrinks every weight a little, Lasso sets most of them to exactly zero, and the reason is the shape of these two distances. Genetic research: tens of thousands of gene expression levels, a few hundred patients. You need a model that says "these eleven genes matter and the rest do not". Only one of these two penalties can produce that answer, and which one is decided by the shape below.

L1 (Manhattan / taxicab) L2 (Euclidean / crow flies) Formula |x₁| + |x₂| + … √(x₁² + x₂² + …) [4, 3] 7 (blocks by road) 5 (straight through the air) Shape of "all points at distance 3" Diamond Circle Outliers More tolerant Squares them, so one big error dominates As a training penalty Pushes weights exactly to 0 → Lasso Shrinks all weights a bit → Ridge / weight decay  Distance = subtract, then pick a norm a = [6,2], b = [2,5]  →  a − b = [4, −3]
L2 distance = 5     L1 distance = 7 Distance is a two-step operation and it is worth keeping them separate in your head: first subtract to get the arrow between the points, then measure that arrow with a norm. The subtraction is the same either way; only the ruler changes. L1 = taxi in Kolkata traffic, only along streets. L2 = a crow over the rooftops. And the diamond has sharp corners sitting on the axes. That's why L1 lands weights exactly on zero. Why the corners matter Here is the argument in full, because it is the one that makes Module 4's Ridge-versus-Lasso table stop being a thing to memorise. Both penalties say: find the weights that fit the data well, subject to the weight vector being no bigger than some budget. The set of weight vectors inside the budget is a circle for L2 and a diamond for L1. The best-fitting solution is wherever the data's own contours first touch that boundary. A circle is smooth, so the contours generally touch it at some ordinary point where both coordinates are non-zero — every weight shrinks, none vanishes. A diamond has corners, and the corners sit exactly on the axes . A corner on the w₁ axis means w₂ = 0. Contours touch corners disproportionately often, because a corner sticks out. That is the whole mechanism: Lasso produces zeros because its constraint region has points on the axes, and Ridge does not because its does not. The same fact read through the gradient: near zero, L2's push (gradient 2w) fades away to nothing, so a small weight is left alone. L1's push stays the same size however small w gets, so it shoves small weights all the way to zero and holds them there. Two tellings of one story. both norms, and the shapes they describe import numpy as np

a, b = np.array([6, 2]), np.array([2, 5])
d = a - b                              # [4, -3]

np.linalg.norm(d)                      # L2 -> 5.0
np.linalg.norm(d, ord=1)               # L1 -> 7.0
np.linalg.norm(d, ord=np.inf)          # L-infinity -> 4.0 (the biggest single step)

# "all points at L1 distance 3" is a diamond; at L2 distance 3, a circle.
theta = np.linspace(0, 2 * np.pi, 400)
circle = np.c_[3 * np.cos(theta), 3 * np.sin(theta)]        # L2 ball
