docs.text: The lab below is the next chapter's subject, but it is worth a minute here: move w and watch the tilt change, move b and watch the whole thing slide sideways without changing shape. Weights set the tilt, bias sets the height — visible in two sliders. interactive lab sigmoid

docs.chapterTitle: From a biological neuron to w·x + b
docs.text:
dataset cancer one neuron, 30 inputs, and the bias trick import numpy as np
from sklearn.linear_model import LinearRegression

model = LinearRegression().fit(X_train, y_train)
print(model.coef_.shape, model.intercept_.round(4))   # (25,) and one bias

# The same model with the bias folded in as a constant feature
Xb = np.c_[np.ones(len(X_train)), X_train]            # prepend a column of 1s
w  = np.linalg.solve(Xb.T @ Xb, Xb.T @ y_train)       # closed form, bias included

print("w0 (the bias) :", w[0].round(4))
print("sklearn bias  :", model.intercept_.round(4))   # identical
print("weights agree :", np.allclose(w[1:], model.coef_))

# Which features pull hardest toward malignant? (valid because X is scaled)
import pandas as pd
pd.Series(model.coef_, index=X_train.columns).sort_values(key=abs, ascending=False).head(5) The two biases print the same number, which is the constant-feature trick demonstrated rather than asserted. The last line is only meaningful because step 4 of the pipeline scaled the columns. Run the final line and keep the answer. The features with the largest positive weights are the ones pushing a prediction towards malignant, and in Module 6 the decision tree will choose its first split from roughly the same group. When two very different model families agree about which features matter, that is the strongest evidence you get from a dataset this size.

docs.chapterTitle: From a biological neuron to w·x + b
docs.text: Draw the four XOR points on paper and try to separate them with one straight line. Success: you can state in one sentence why no line works, without mentioning training. Fit a linear model to the XOR table and report its accuracy. Success: you get 50% and you expected it. Add the feature x₁·x₂ to XOR and refit. Success: 100%, and you can say what that third feature did geometrically. Verify the constant-feature trick on the breast-cancer data with the code above. Success: w[0] equals model.intercept_ and the remaining weights match. Stretch goals Implement the 1943 McCulloch–Pitts neuron — binary inputs, weights of +1 and −1, fire if the sum meets a threshold — and build AND, OR and NOT with it. Then try to build XOR and watch exactly where it fails. Fit a linear model to the breast-cancer data with and without the intercept ( fit_intercept=False ) and compare. The gap is what the bias was doing.

docs.chapterTitle: From a biological neuron to w·x + b
docs.text: 43 fires, 49 wires, 58 learns, 69 burns. Weights set the tilt. Bias sets the height. Append a column of ones and the bias becomes just another weight. XOR fails because no line exists, not because training was too short. Fix it by adding features or by stacking layers. What does the bias term do, and how can you get rid of it? It is the intercept — without it the line is forced through the origin. Add a constant feature x₀ = 1 and the bias becomes the weight w₀, making the model a pure dot product. Why can one perceptron not learn XOR? XOR's two positive points lie on one diagonal and its two negatives on the other, so no single straight line separates them. The solution is outside the model's hypothesis space, so no amount of training reaches it. What happened in 1969 and why did it matter? Minsky and Papert published the XOR limitation of a single perceptron, funding dried up and the first AI winter began. Stacking layers resolved the limitation later. You see a weight of 0.0001 on a feature. Is it unimportant? Not necessarily — weights carry the units of their feature. On unscaled data a tiny weight on a large-magnitude column can dominate. Only compare coefficients after scaling.

docs.sectionTitle: Why a straight-line model can draw a curve
docs.text: Add powers and products of features (x², x³, x₁x₂) and a linear model can bend. It is still linear in the weights, which is why the same solver works — the model never learns that x² is the square of x, it just sees another column. That is a remarkably cheap way to buy flexibility, and it is a remarkably easy way to destroy a model. This chapter is both halves. Model Train Test Linear, degree 1 95.8% 98.2% Linear, degree 3 (thousands of features) 100.0% 75.4% Ridge, degree 3 (α = 10⁴) 90.5% 90.4% Lasso, degree 3 (40 active weights) 96.9% 96.5% Logistic regression 97.1% 98.2% On the breast-cancer data. 100% train with 75% test is the textbook signature of overfitting: the model memorised. Read row 2 as arithmetic rather than as a surprise. Degree 3 on 25 scaled features generates every cube, every square, every pairwise and triple product — thousands of columns — against about 455 training rows. With more parameters than examples a linear model can fit the training set exactly, and exactly is what it does.

docs.sectionTitle: Live: degree up, then penalty up
docs.text: Raise the degree to 11 with the penalty off. Watch training error collapse, test error climb, and ‖w‖ run into the thousands. Then raise α and watch all three come back — that is the entire chapter in two sliders. interactive lab poly

Ridge (L2) and Lasso (L1) Ridge:  minimise   Σ(y − ŷ)²  +  α Σ wⱼ²
Lasso:  minimise   (1/2n) Σ(y − ŷ)²  +  α Σ |wⱼ| Both add a price for large weights. The fit still wants to match the data; the penalty still wants every weight near zero; α decides who wins. At α = 0 you have plain least squares. At α → ∞ every weight goes to zero and the model predicts the mean.  Ridge (L2) Lasso (L1) Penalty sum of squared weights sum of absolute weights Effect shrinks every weight, none to exactly 0 sets many weights to exactly 0 → automatic feature selection Pick when most features help a little, often correlated you suspect only a few features matter (genes, text words) Strength α larger = stronger penalty = simpler model α larger = stronger penalty = simpler model  Ridge Reduces. Lasso Lops off. L1's diamond-shaped constraint has corners on the axes; the best solution usually hits a corner, which means some weights are exactly 0. L2's circle has no corners. Why does L1 zero things? Near zero, L2's push (gradient 2w) fades to nothing; L1's push stays the same size, so small weights get shoved all the way to 0 and held there. The geometry version — the diamond's corners sitting on the axes — is in the norms chapter , and the two arguments are the same fact told from different ends. Elastic Net, briefly Both penalties at once ElasticNet:  minimise  (1/2n) Σ(y − ŷ)²  +  α [ ρ·Σ|wⱼ|  +  (1−ρ)/2·Σwⱼ² ]
ρ = l1_ratio:  1 → pure Lasso,  0 → pure Ridge The reason it exists: given a group of strongly correlated features, Lasso picks one more or less arbitrarily and zeroes the rest, which makes the selection unstable across resamples. Adding a little L2 makes correlated features shrink together , so the group survives or dies as a group. When your features come in natural families — the _mean , _se and _worst versions of each nucleus measurement, say — that is usually what you want. In LogisticRegression and SVMs, the knob is C = 1/strength . Smaller C = stronger regularisation. It runs the opposite way to α. Getting this backwards is the single most common tuning error in the course. α is the penalty; C is the patience for data. Raise α and the model gets simpler. Raise C and it gets more complex. Same knob, read from opposite ends. Genetic research: tens of thousands of gene expression levels, a few hundred patients. Lasso picks the handful of genes linked to a disease. House prices: dozens of mildly useful, correlated features (rooms, area, floors), so Ridge keeps them all, gently shrunk. L2 regularisation in deep learning is "weight decay", a standard setting when fine-tuning LLMs. the three fits from the table from sklearn.preprocessing import PolynomialFeatures, StandardScaler
from sklearn.pipeline import make_pipeline
from sklearn.linear_model import LinearRegression, Ridge, Lasso
import numpy as np

# y01: 1 = malignant, 0 = benign  (X_train / X_test already cleaned and scaled)
for name, reg in [("plain", LinearRegression()),
                  ("ridge", Ridge(alpha=1e4)),
                  ("lasso", Lasso(alpha=0.023, max_iter=200))]:
    model = make_pipeline(PolynomialFeatures(3, include_bias=False), StandardScaler(), reg)
    model.fit(X_train, y_train01)
    acc_tr = ((model.predict(X_train) >= 0.5) == y_train01).mean()
    acc_te = ((model.predict(X_test)  >= 0.5) == y_test01).mean()
    print(name, round(acc_tr, 3), round(acc_te, 3))

lasso = model[-1]
print("weights switched off:", np.sum(lasso.coef_ == 0), "of", lasso.coef_.size) The second StandardScaler, after PolynomialFeatures, is not redundant: cubing a scaled column produces a column with a completely different spread, and a penalty applied to weights on unscaled columns penalises them unequally. That last point is worth stating plainly, because it is a real trap. A penalty of α on every weight is only fair if every feature is on the same scale — otherwise the weight on a large-magnitude column is naturally small and barely penalised, while the weight on a small-magnitude column is naturally large and crushed. Always scale before regularising.

Regularising without scaling. The penalty is then unequal across features, as above. This is the most consequential mistake in the chapter. Penalising the intercept. It is not a slope and shrinking it towards zero biases the predictions. scikit-learn excludes it by default; a hand-rolled implementation must too. Tuning α on test. Use RidgeCV , LassoCV or an explicit cross-validation inside the training half. Reading Lasso's survivors as 'the important features'. Given correlated columns it keeps one arbitrarily. The survivors are a sufficient set, not the important set. Lasso not converging. max_iter=200 is low. If you see a ConvergenceWarning, raise it rather than ignoring it, or scale better. Expecting polynomial features to help. They help when the true boundary is curved and the features are few. Neither is true here. ISLP Ch 6 ISLP chapter 6 is the authoritative treatment: the constraint-region picture, the bias–variance explanation of why shrinkage helps, and the comparison between subset selection, Ridge and Lasso on the same data.

dataset cancer The table at the top of this chapter is the result to reproduce. Three things in it are worth reading closely: Degree 3, no penalty: 100% train, 75.4% test. A 24.6-point gap. Ridge at α = 10⁴: the gap closes to 0.1 points, but both numbers fall to ~90% — the penalty is too strong and has underfit. Lasso with 40 surviving weights: 96.9% and 96.5%, a 0.4-point gap, and it got there by discarding thousands of features. Lasso wins here because most of those polynomial columns genuinely carry nothing. And the quiet lesson in rows 1 and 5: plain degree-1 linear regression and logistic regression both hit 98.2%, beating every regularised polynomial. The extra flexibility was never needed. Try the simple thing first is not advice about effort, it is advice about accuracy. Take-home answers (from the notebook) 1. Why didn't polynomial features help? The breast-cancer classes are already nearly linearly separable in 20–30 scaled features. Degree 3 explodes the feature count into the thousands with only ~455 training rows, so the model fits noise. Polynomials win when the true boundary is curved and features are few, e.g. make_moons or make_circles from sklearn. 2. Polynomial logistic regression: PolynomialFeatures(degree=2) , fit_transform on train, transform on test, then LogisticRegression(C=...) . As C drops 1 → 0.1 → 0.01 the penalty grows, train accuracy falls, and the train/test gap closes. Adding a StandardScaler after the polynomial step helps the solver converge. 3. RidgeCV: make_pipeline(PolynomialFeatures(3, include_bias=False), StandardScaler(), RidgeCV(alphas=alphas)) fit on train. CV picks a smaller α than 10⁴ and test accuracy beats the hand-picked 90.4%.

Reproduce all five rows of the table on the cleaned breast-cancer data. Success: your degree-3 plain fit shows a train/test gap above 20 points. Count how many Lasso weights are exactly zero at α = 0.023. Success: roughly 40 survive out of thousands, and you can state what fraction that is. Replace the hand-picked α = 10⁴ with RidgeCV over a log-spaced grid. Success: CV picks something smaller and test accuracy improves on 90.4%. Sweep LogisticRegression 's C from 1 → 0.1 → 0.01 and tabulate train and test accuracy. Success: you can state which direction C moves complexity, having just watched it. Stretch goals Run the whole comparison once with the second StandardScaler removed. The degradation is the size of the scale-before-you-penalise rule. Fit ElasticNetCV over a grid of l1_ratio and compare its surviving feature set with Lasso's across three different random splits. Lasso's set should be noticeably less stable. Build make_circles data and show polynomial features turning an impossible problem into an easy one — the case where this technique is actually the right tool.

Polynomial features make a model bend while staying linear in the weights. Ridge Reduces. Lasso Lops off. α up = simpler. C up = more complex. They point opposite ways. Always scale before regularising, or the penalty is unequal across features. Degree 1 and logistic both beat every polynomial here — try the simple thing first. What does a 100% train / 75% test result tell you? The model memorised the training set. Reduce complexity, add regularisation, select features, or get more data. The gap is the diagnosis, not either number. Why does Lasso produce exact zeros and Ridge does not? L1's gradient keeps its magnitude as a weight approaches zero, so small weights get pushed all the way; L2's push fades to nothing. Geometrically, L1's constraint region is a diamond with corners on the axes. Which way does C go, compared with α? Opposite. α is the penalty, so larger α means a simpler model. C is the inverse of the penalty, so larger C means a more complex model. Why scale features before applying a penalty? The penalty charges per unit of weight, and weights carry their feature's units. Without scaling, large-magnitude columns are barely penalised and small-magnitude ones are crushed.

docs.chapterTitle: Logistic regression and the decision threshold
docs.sectionTitle: Why a linear model is not quite enough
docs.text: The Module 3 pipeline classified tumours with plain linear regression on a −1/+1 label, and it worked — 98.2%. So why learn another model? Because the output is not a probability. A prediction of 2.4 is not "140% malignant". There is no sensible way to say "flag this one for review if the model is at least 80% sure", because the model is not expressing certainty at all. And as soon as the cost of a miss differs from the cost of a false alarm — which is always, in medicine — you need that dial. Logistic regression keeps the linear score and adds one step: squash it into (0, 1). That one step buys calibrated probabilities, a principled loss, and a threshold you can move on purpose.

docs.chapterTitle: Logistic regression and the decision threshold
docs.text:
Sigmoid squashes any number into (0, 1) z = w·x + b
P(y = 1 | x) = σ(z) = 1 / (1 + e⁻ᶻ)
σ(0) = 0.5     σ(large +) → 1     σ(large −) → 0 Read the formula at three points and it stops being mysterious. At z = 0 the exponent is e⁰ = 1, so σ = 1/2 — maximum uncertainty. At large positive z, e⁻ᶻ collapses to nearly zero, so σ → 1. At large negative z, e⁻ᶻ explodes, so σ → 0. The S-shape is just those three facts joined smoothly. interactive lab sigmoid  Odds = P / (1 − P). A 0.8 chance means odds of 4 to 1. Take the log and something neat appears: log(odds) = z = w·x + b . Logistic regression is a linear model of the log-odds, which is why it's still called "regression". The three readings of the same model log-odds:    log(p / (1 − p)) = w·x + b      ← linear in x
odds:        p / (1 − p)       = e^(w·x + b)     ← multiplicative
probability: p                 = 1/(1 + e^−(w·x+b))  ← the S-curve The middle line is how you interpret a coefficient. A weight of 1.73 on petal length means: each extra unit of petal length multiplies the odds of the positive class by e^1.73 ≈ 5.6. Not the probability — the odds. That distinction is what makes logistic coefficients reportable to a domain expert. Linear regression draws the line. Logistic regression bends it into an S and reads it as a probability.  The boundary is still straight Boundary: predict class 1 when σ(z) ≥ 0.5, i.e. when z ≥ 0. Since z is linear, the boundary is a straight line. Want a circle? Make z quadratic: z = w₀ + w₁x₁² + w₂x₂². Feature engineering changes the boundary shape. This is the point people miss: the sigmoid is not what makes the model flexible. It only converts a score to a probability. The shape of the decision boundary is decided entirely by what goes into z — which is why logistic regression is a linear classifier despite its curve. Loss: log-loss (binary cross-entropy). sklearn adds an L2 penalty by default (C = 1.0) and solves with lbfgs , a faster cousin of gradient descent, because there's no closed form. scikit-learn's LogisticRegression is regularised by default , at C = 1.0. It is not plain maximum-likelihood logistic regression unless you ask for it. If your coefficients disagree with a statistics textbook's, this is usually why. Moving the decision threshold predict() uses 0.5. In cancer screening a miss is far worse than a false alarm, so lower it: recall rises, precision falls. Use predict_proba(X)[:, 1] and pick the threshold on validation data, never on test. interactive lab threshold  0.5 is not a law of nature. It is the point where the two classes are equally probable, which is only the right operating point if the two mistakes cost the same. They almost never do. Choosing the threshold is a separate decision from fitting the model, and it belongs to whoever owns the cost — not to the default argument of a function. fit, then sweep the threshold from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression
import numpy as np

lr = LogisticRegression(max_iter=500, C=1.0).fit(X_train, y_train01)
probs = lr.predict_proba(X_test)[:, 1]          # P(malignant) for each patient

for t in [0.5, 0.4, 0.3, 0.2, 0.1]:
    pred = (probs >= t).astype(int)
    missed = ((pred == 0) & (y_test01 == 1)).sum()
    alarms = ((pred == 1) & (y_test01 == 0)).sum()
    print(t, "missed", missed, "false alarms", alarms)

# Reading a coefficient as an odds multiplier
import pandas as pd
pd.Series(np.exp(lr.coef_[0]), index=X_train.columns) \
  .sort_values(ascending=False).head(5).round(3) `predict_proba` returns two columns, one per class; `[:, 1]` takes the positive class. The last block exponentiates the coefficients so they read as 'multiplies the odds by'.

docs.chapterTitle: Logistic regression and the decision threshold
docs.text: Perfect separation. If a feature separates the classes exactly, the likelihood is maximised by driving its weight to infinity. You get huge coefficients and a convergence warning. The default L2 penalty is what normally prevents it. Reading a coefficient as a probability change. It is a log-odds change. Exponentiate it to get an odds multiplier. Unscaled features. The solver converges badly and the coefficients are not comparable. Scale first — and with the default penalty, scaling is required for the penalty to be fair. Tuning the threshold on test. The threshold is a parameter. Pick it on validation. Trusting the probabilities without checking calibration. Logistic regression is usually well calibrated, but a regularised model on imbalanced data may not be. Plot predicted probability against observed frequency before you promise anyone a percentage. max_iter too low. The default 100 is often not enough. 500 or 1000 costs nothing here. ISLP Ch 4 ISLP chapter 4 derives logistic regression from maximum likelihood, explains the odds interpretation carefully, and contrasts it with LDA and naive Bayes — which make distributional assumptions logistic regression does not.

docs.chapterTitle: Logistic regression and the decision threshold
docs.text: Two real results from the course, on two different datasets. Where Setting Result Week 1 notebook, breast cancer Logistic regression on 25 cleaned, scaled features train 97.1%, test 98.2% Assignment Q10, iris (setosa vs virginica) Four features, 80/20 split, random_state=42 coef_ = [0.46, −0.31, 1.73 , 0.81], intercept_ = −8.35, accuracy 1.0  Why the iris accuracy is 1.0: setosa and virginica are the two most different species, so they are linearly separable in these four features. Petal length has the largest weight (1.73), which is consistent with what the pairplot shows — petal features separate the species best. Exponentiate that weight and each extra centimetre of petal length multiplies the odds of virginica by about 5.6. Assignment-1 Part 2 (Q6–Q10) builds exactly this. The graded details: LabelEncoder maps classes alphabetically (setosa 0, versicolor 1, virginica 2), so you drop versicolor with data[data.Species != 1] and relabel virginica with .replace(2, 1) to get a binary problem with 50 of each class. The split is test_size=0.2, random_state=42 → train (80, 4), test (20, 4). Print the weights and the bias, not just the accuracy. dataset cancer

docs.chapterTitle: Logistic regression and the decision threshold
docs.text: Reproduce Assignment Q6–Q10 on iris: encode labels, drop versicolor, relabel, split 80/20 with random_state=42 , fit, print coef_ and intercept_ and accuracy. Success: coefficients ≈ [0.46, −0.31, 1.73, 0.81], intercept ≈ −8.35, accuracy 1.0. Draw the pairplot with hue="Species" and confirm by eye that petal features separate best. Success: your explanation of the 1.73 weight cites the plot. Fit logistic regression on the cleaned breast-cancer features and sweep the threshold 0.5 → 0.1. Success: a table of missed tumours against false alarms, and a recommended threshold with a one-sentence justification. Exponentiate the breast-cancer coefficients and report the top five as odds multipliers. Success: you can phrase one of them as a sentence a doctor would understand. Stretch goals Some tumours stay missed even at threshold 0.2, because the model gives them near-zero probability. Find them and look at their features — they look benign in these measurements, so only better features or a different model would help. Plot a calibration curve: bucket the predicted probabilities and plot each bucket's mean prediction against its observed malignant rate. A well-calibrated model sits on the diagonal. Fit a polynomial logistic regression with PolynomialFeatures(degree=2) and sweep C from 1 → 0.1 → 0.01, watching the train/test gap close.

docs.chapterTitle: Logistic regression and the decision threshold
docs.text: Linear regression draws the line; logistic bends it into an S and reads it as a probability. log(odds) = w·x + b — which is why a classifier is called a regression. A coefficient is a log-odds change; exponentiate it for an odds multiplier. The boundary is still straight, because z is still linear. Only feature engineering bends it. 0.5 is a default, not a law. Pick the threshold from the cost, on validation data. Why is logistic "regression" a classifier? It regresses a linear score on the log-odds scale, then the sigmoid converts that score into a class probability. The regression is of log(p/(1−p)), which is linear in x. What happens to precision and recall as you lower the threshold? Recall rises and precision falls — you flag more cases, catching more true positives and more false alarms. There is no threshold that improves both. A coefficient is 1.73. What does that mean? Each one-unit increase in that feature adds 1.73 to the log-odds, which multiplies the odds of the positive class by e^1.73 ≈ 5.6. It is not a change in probability. Why is the decision boundary straight even though the sigmoid is curved? The boundary is where σ(z) = 0.5, i.e. z = 0, and z = w·x + b is linear in x. The sigmoid only maps scores to probabilities; it does not change the boundary's shape.

Linear regression has a closed form. Logistic regression does not, and neither does an SVM, a neural network, or anything you will meet after this course. For all of those, "find the weights that minimise the loss" is not a formula you evaluate — it is a search you run. Gradient descent is that search, and it is almost embarrassingly simple: work out which way is downhill, take a small step that way, repeat. Everything sophisticated in modern training — Adam, momentum, learning-rate schedules — is a refinement of those two lines.

The derivative tells you the slope. Positive slope → moving right goes uphill, so move left. Negative slope → move right. At a minimum the slope is 0. Update rule w  ←  w − η · dL/dw          (η = learning rate, η > 0)
Why it works: L(w + h) − L(w) ≈ L'(w)·h. With h = −η L'(w),
the change is −η L'(w)² ≤ 0. The loss can only go down (for small η). That justification is worth reading twice, because it is the whole guarantee and it is three lines. Take a first-order Taylor expansion of the loss. Substitute the step we intend to take. The resulting change is minus a positive number times a square — and a square is never negative. So the loss decreases. The only caveat is "for small η", because the Taylor approximation is only good nearby, and that caveat is exactly where divergence comes from. interactive lab gd  The slope says which way. The learning rate says how big a stride. Too small: you're still walking at sunrise. Too big: you leap over the valley and bounce up the other side. More than one weight: partial derivatives and the gradient The lab has one weight. A real model has many — logistic regression on the cancer data has 25 weights and a bias. The loss is then a surface over many dimensions, and you need the slope in each direction separately. That slope is a partial derivative : change one weight, freeze all the others, measure how fast the loss changes. Collect one partial derivative per weight into a vector and you have the gradient ∇L, which points steepest uphill. The update becomes wᵢ ← wᵢ − η·∂L/∂wᵢ for every weight at once. If derivatives are new to you, the calculus chapter builds them from scratch, with worked examples and labs for slopes, partial derivatives and the chain rule. interactive lab partial The same descent on a two-weight loss. Each side panel is a slice of the surface; its slope is one partial derivative. Try the long valley with a large step to see the zig-zag. The two gradients to know Gradients you should know Linear regression (MSE):     ∂L/∂w = (2/n) Σ (ŷᵢ − yᵢ) xᵢ
Logistic regression (log-loss): ∂L/∂w = (1/n) Σ (pᵢ − yᵢ) xᵢ
Same shape: (prediction − truth) × input. The fact that these two are the same shape is not a coincidence, and it is the most useful thing in this chapter. Two completely different losses, applied to two different models, produce the same update form: error times input . A feature that was large on an example the model got badly wrong gets a large correction. A feature that was zero gets none. This generalises. Backpropagation through a deep network is this same quantity, chained. If you understand "error times input" you have the shape of nearly all gradient-based learning. When to stop, and where you land When to stop: after a fixed number of iterations, or when the weights (or loss) barely change between two iterations. Local vs global minima: MSE for linear regression and log-loss for logistic regression are convex (one bowl), so gradient descent finds the global minimum. Neural networks have many dips. Convexity is why every model in this course has a reproducible answer. Run logistic regression twice from different starting points and you get the same weights. Run a neural network twice and you do not — and that is the single biggest practical difference between the two worlds. Batch, stochastic, mini-batch Variant Uses per step Trade-off Batch GD All rows Smooth but slow on big data Stochastic GD One row Fast, noisy path Mini-batch GD 32 / 64 / 128 rows The default in deep learning  The noise in stochastic descent is not purely a cost. On a non-convex surface it can shake the search out of a shallow dip that batch descent would settle into — which is part of why mini-batch became the default rather than a compromise. gradient descent for linear regression, from scratch import numpy as np

def gd(X, y, lr=0.1, steps=500):
    X = np.c_[np.ones(len(X)), X]          # bias as weight w0
    w = np.zeros(X.shape[1])
    for _ in range(steps):
        grad = 2 / len(X) * X.T @ (X @ w - y)
        w -= lr * grad
    return w

# Check it against the closed form
w_gd = gd(X_train.to_numpy(), y_train, lr=0.1, steps=2000)
Xb = np.c_[np.ones(len(X_train)), X_train]
w_exact = np.linalg.solve(Xb.T @ Xb, Xb.T @ y_train)
print(np.abs(w_gd - w_exact).max().round(6))   # -> tiny, if lr and steps are sane `X @ w - y` is the error vector and `X.T @ error` is error-times-input summed over rows — the formula above, written in one line of linear algebra. Run that comparison and the agreement is the proof. Iterating towards the answer and solving for it directly land in the same place, because the surface is convex and there is only one place to land.

Learning rate too high. The loss increases, oscillates, or becomes nan . On the simple bowl L(w) = w² the threshold is exactly η = 1 — the lab lets you cross it on purpose. Learning rate too low. The loss falls but never arrives. Looks like a modelling problem; is a patience problem. Always plot loss against iteration. Unscaled features. If one feature's scale is a thousand times another's, the loss surface is a long narrow valley and a single learning rate cannot suit both directions. Gradient descent zigzags. Scaling is not optional here. Forgetting to average. Dividing by n keeps the gradient's size independent of the dataset size, so your learning rate still works when the data grows. Expecting reproducibility from a non-convex model. Different initialisation, different minimum. Fix the seed and report it. ISLP Ch 4 ISLP chapter 4 covers the maximum-likelihood fitting of logistic regression that this iteration is solving, and its deep-learning chapter returns to gradient descent with momentum and the stochastic variants.

dataset cancer a learning-rate sweep on the real features import numpy as np

def gd_trace(X, y, lr, steps=300):
    X = np.c_[np.ones(len(X)), X]
    w = np.zeros(X.shape[1])
    losses = []
    for _ in range(steps):
        err = X @ w - y
        losses.append((err ** 2).mean())
        w -= lr * (2 / len(X)) * (X.T @ err)
    return np.array(losses), w

Xtr = X_train.to_numpy()
for lr in [0.001, 0.01, 0.1, 0.5, 1.0]:
    losses, _ = gd_trace(Xtr, y_train, lr)
    end = losses[-1]
    print(f"lr={lr:<6} final loss {end:.4f}  "
          f"{'DIVERGED' if not np.isfinite(end) or end > losses[0] else 'ok'}") Plot each `losses` curve on one set of axes. The small rates give long slow slopes, the good one drops fast and flattens, and the largest blows up — three shapes you will recognise for the rest of your career. This works on the cleaned, scaled features from the Module 3 pipeline. Try it on the raw columns, where area_worst runs into the thousands, and every learning rate that is stable for one feature is useless for another. That experiment is the most convincing argument for scaling you will run.

Implement gd from scratch and check it against np.linalg.solve on the breast-cancer features. Success: the maximum absolute difference is below 1e-4 and you can say why it is not exactly zero. Sweep the learning rate over five orders of magnitude and plot loss against iteration for each. Success: you can point at the too-small, the good and the diverging curve. Find the exact divergence threshold for L(w) = w² by hand. Success: you derive η = 1 from the update w ← w(1 − 2η) and confirm it in the lab. Derive the logistic gradient from log-loss and the sigmoid. Success: you arrive at (1/n) Σ (pᵢ − yᵢ) xᵢ and can say why the sigmoid's derivative cancels so neatly. Stretch goals Implement stochastic and mini-batch variants and plot all three loss curves together. The noise in the stochastic path should be clearly visible. Run the sweep on unscaled features and find a single learning rate that works for all 30 columns. You will not find one — that is the result. Add momentum: keep a running average of the gradient and step along that instead. Compare how many iterations each needs to reach the same loss.

The slope says which way; the learning rate says how big a stride. Both gradients have the same shape: (prediction − truth) × input. The guarantee is three lines of Taylor expansion, and it only holds for small η. Convex loss → one minimum → reproducible answer. Neural networks have many dips. Unscaled features make a narrow valley that no single learning rate suits. Write the gradient-descent update rule and say why it decreases the loss. w ← w − η·dL/dw. From a first-order expansion, the change in loss is approximately −η·L'(w)², which is never positive — so for a small enough η the loss can only go down. What happens if the learning rate is too large? The step overshoots the minimum and lands further up the other side, so the loss grows each iteration and eventually becomes infinite. On L(w) = w² this happens for η above 1. Why do the MSE and log-loss gradients have the same shape? Both reduce to (prediction − truth) × input. For log-loss the sigmoid's derivative cancels against the log in the loss, leaving the same error-times-input form — which is also the shape backpropagation generalises. Does gradient descent find the global minimum? For a convex loss — MSE in linear regression, log-loss in logistic regression — yes, there is only one. For a neural network, no: there are many dips and where you land depends on initialisation.

docs.sectionTitle: Why 'any line that works' is not good enough
docs.moduleTitle: Linear classifiers, SVM, bias vs variance
docs.text: Many lines can split two classes. An SVM picks the one with the widest empty street on both sides, because that line survives noise best. This chapter builds the first half of that sentence. The perceptron finds a line — the first one that happens to work, often one scraping past a point by a hair. Next chapter explains why that is a problem and what to do instead. Starting here rather than with the SVM is worth the detour, because the perceptron's update rule is three lines long, it is the direct ancestor of backpropagation, and watching it stop at an obviously bad line is the most convincing possible motivation for margins.

docs.moduleTitle: Linear classifiers, SVM, bias vs variance
docs.text:
Supervised learning, framed Features : any measurable attribute (numeric, categorical, ordinal). Model : an imagined relation between features and label, with parameters. There is no "true model" hiding in the data, only better and worse descriptions. Learning algorithm : anything that estimates those parameters by minimising a loss. That middle sentence is the one to sit with. Students often look for the right model as though it were a fact about the data waiting to be discovered. It is not. A model is a description you propose, and the question is only whether it describes well enough to be useful on data you have not seen. Model family Form Linear regression Y = w₀ + w₁X₁ + w₂X₂ + w₃X₃ Polynomial / interaction Y = w₀ + w₁X₁ + w₂X₂² + w₃X₂X₃ Linear classifier Y = sign(w₀ + w₁X₁ + w₂X₂ + w₃X₃) Logistic regression P(Y=1|X) = 1 / (1 + exp(−w·X))  A line in 2D, a hyperplane in D dimensions The compact form w₁x₁ + w₂x₂ + w₃ = 0     (w₃ is the bias, weight of a constant feature 1)
compact: W·X = 0, with W and X both (D + 1)-dimensional
prediction: y = sign(W·X)  → +1 on one side, −1 on the other This is the constant-feature trick from Module 4, now doing real work: folding the bias into W means the boundary is the clean statement W·X = 0 rather than w·x + b = 0 , and the perceptron update below becomes a single line instead of two. Linearly separable : at least one line splits the classes perfectly. Many real datasets are not. Geometrically, W is the normal to the boundary — it points perpendicular to the line, towards the +1 side — and W·X is proportional to the signed distance from a point to that line. The sign is which side; the magnitude is how far. A linear classifier needs numeric features. Categories must be encoded first (one-hot) before the dot product means anything. The perceptron algorithm Perceptron start with any W
repeat over the data:
    if yᵢ · (W·Xᵢ) ≤ 0:      # wrong side (or on the line)
        W = W + yᵢ Xᵢ          # nudge the line toward the right answer
stop when every point is correct (or after max_iter) The test yᵢ·(W·Xᵢ) ≤ 0 is the whole cleverness. W·Xᵢ is positive on one side and negative on the other; yᵢ is +1 or −1. Multiply them and the product is positive exactly when the prediction and the label agree. So one expression covers both classes with no case analysis. Why the update works: if a +1 point scored negative, adding Xᵢ to W raises W·Xᵢ by |Xᵢ|². If the data is linearly separable, the perceptron is guaranteed to find a perfect line in finitely many steps. If not, it never settles. The perceptron is a student who only studies the questions they got wrong. Correct points contribute nothing to the update. All the learning comes from mistakes — which is also why it stops the instant there are none. interactive lab svm  Run the perceptron twice in that lab, from different starting states, and you will usually get two different lines. Both are correct on the training data. Neither has any claim to being better — which is precisely the gap the next chapter closes.

docs.moduleTitle: Linear classifiers, SVM, bias vs variance
docs.text: Non-separable data. The perceptron never converges — it cycles forever, swapping which points it gets wrong. You must cap max_iter , and the line you end on is whichever one the clock stopped at. No margin guarantee. It stops at the first working line, which may pass within a hair of a training point. One noisy new observation then flips that point. Order dependence. Shuffle the rows and you get a different line. Reproducibility requires fixing both the order and the initialisation. Unscaled features. The update adds yᵢXᵢ directly to W, so a feature measured in thousands dominates every step. No probabilities. The output is a sign. If you need confidence, use logistic regression. ISLP Ch 9 ISLP chapter 9 opens with the maximal margin classifier for exactly the reason this chapter ends on: among the infinitely many separating hyperplanes, some principled choice has to be made, and 'widest margin' is that principle.

docs.moduleTitle: Linear classifiers, SVM, bias vs variance
docs.text:
dataset cancer the perceptron, written out, on the real features import numpy as np

def perceptron(X, y, max_iter=100):
    """y must be -1/+1. Returns W including the bias as W[0]."""
    X = np.c_[np.ones(len(X)), X]              # constant feature -> bias folded in
    W = np.zeros(X.shape[1])
    for epoch in range(max_iter):
        mistakes = 0
        for xi, yi in zip(X, y):
            if yi * (W @ xi) <= 0:             # wrong side, or exactly on the line
                W += yi * xi                   # the entire learning rule
                mistakes += 1
        if mistakes == 0:
            return W, epoch + 1
    return W, max_iter

W, epochs = perceptron(X_train.to_numpy(), y_train)   # y_train is -1/+1
print("converged in", epochs, "passes")

Xb_test = np.c_[np.ones(len(X_test)), X_test]
pred = np.where(Xb_test @ W > 0, 1, -1)
print("test accuracy", (pred == y_test).mean().round(4))

# Run it again on shuffled rows: a different line, also correct on train
idx = np.random.default_rng(0).permutation(len(X_train))
W2, _ = perceptron(X_train.to_numpy()[idx], y_train[idx])
print("same line?", np.allclose(W, W2))        # -> False The last two lines are the lesson. Two runs, two different boundaries, both perfect on the training data. The perceptron has no way to prefer one.

docs.moduleTitle: Linear classifiers, SVM, bias vs variance
docs.text: Implement the perceptron from the pseudocode and run it on the cleaned breast-cancer features. Success: it converges in a handful of passes and you report test accuracy. Run it on shuffled data three times and compare the resulting W vectors. Success: they differ, and you can say why that matters. Construct deliberately non-separable data (overlap two blobs) and run with max_iter=1000 . Success: it never reaches zero mistakes, and you can describe what the mistake count does instead. Verify the update's effect by hand: take a misclassified +1 point, apply W += X, and show that W·X increased by |X|². Success: your arithmetic matches. Stretch goals Track and plot the number of mistakes per pass for both separable and non-separable data. One curve hits zero; the other plateaus and jitters forever. Add a learning rate to the update ( W += lr * yi * xi ) and show it changes only the scale of W, not the boundary — a useful demonstration that the perceptron's boundary is scale-invariant in W.

docs.moduleTitle: Linear classifiers, SVM, bias vs variance
docs.text: There is no true model hiding in the data — only better and worse descriptions. W·X = 0 is the boundary; W is its normal, and W·X is the signed distance. yᵢ·(W·Xᵢ) ≤ 0 covers both classes in one expression. The perceptron only studies the questions it got wrong. It stops at the first line that works — which is the problem the SVM solves. State the perceptron update rule and when it fires. If yᵢ(W·Xᵢ) ≤ 0 — the point is on the wrong side or exactly on the line — then W ← W + yᵢXᵢ. Correctly classified points produce no update. Is the perceptron guaranteed to converge? Only if the data is linearly separable; then it finds a perfect line in finitely many steps. On non-separable data it never settles and must be capped by max_iter. What does W·X represent geometrically? W is the normal to the boundary, and W·X is proportional to the signed perpendicular distance from the point to that boundary — sign gives the side, magnitude the distance. Two perceptron runs give different lines. Which is better? The algorithm cannot say — both are perfect on the training data. That absence of a preference is what motivates the maximum-margin criterion.

docs.chapterTitle: Margins, soft margins and support vectors
docs.sectionTitle: Why width is the right criterion
docs.moduleTitle: Linear classifiers, SVM, bias vs variance
docs.text: The perceptron stops at the first line that works, often one that scrapes past a point. A tiny bit of noise then flips that point. Here is the argument for width, in one step. Your training points are samples. A new point from the same source will land near — but not exactly on — an existing one. If the boundary runs a hair from a training point, a small perturbation crosses it. If the boundary sits in the middle of a wide empty corridor, a small perturbation changes nothing. Width is robustness to the noise you have not seen yet. Pave the widest possible road between two villages. The centre line is the decision boundary, the kerbs are the margins, and the houses touching the kerbs are the support vectors.

docs.chapterTitle: Margins, soft margins and support vectors
docs.moduleTitle: Linear classifiers, SVM, bias vs variance
docs.text:
The margin of a class is the smallest perpendicular distance from any of its points to the line. We want both margins large and equal. From zero: how far is a point from a line? (the geometry the SVM is built on) A line (in 2-D) or hyperplane (in more dimensions) is the set of points where w · x + b = 0 . The vector w is perpendicular to it — it points straight across the street. For any point x, the number f(x) = w · x + b is positive on one side, negative on the other and zero on the line; that sign is the SVM's prediction. Its size is a scaled distance. The true perpendicular distance is |w · x + b| / ‖w‖ . Worked example line: 3x₁ + 4x₂ − 5 = 0      → w = (3, 4), b = −5, ‖w‖ = √(9 + 16) = 5
point (3, 4):   w·x + b = 9 + 16 − 5 = 20     distance = 20 / 5 = 4
point (1, 0.5): w·x + b = 3 + 2 − 5 = 0       distance = 0  (on the line)

kerbs at w·x + b = ±1 → each kerb is 1/‖w‖ = 0.2 from the centre, street width 2/‖w‖ = 0.4
halve w to (1.5, 2), b = −2.5 → same centre line, street width 2/2.5 = 0.8 The last two lines are the whole idea behind “minimise ‖w‖”: the centre line stays put when you scale w and b together, but the kerbs (where f = ±1) move outwards as ‖w‖ shrinks. The SVM looks for the smallest w that still keeps every training point on the correct side of its kerb (y·f(x) ≥ 1). Hinge loss in numbers, for a point whose label is y = +1 f(x) = 2.0   → max(0, 1 − 2.0)  = 0     correct and outside the street: no cost
f(x) = 0.5   → max(0, 1 − 0.5)  = 0.5   correct side, but inside the street
f(x) = −1.0  → max(0, 1 + 1.0)  = 2.0   wrong side: cost grows linearly Max-margin as optimisation boundaries:   W·X = +k (red side)   and   W·X = −k (blue side)
total margin = 2k / ‖W‖
maximise margin ⇔ minimise ½‖W‖²   subject to  yᵢ(W·Xᵢ) ≥ k for every i The flip from "maximise" to "minimise" deserves unpacking, because it is where students lose the thread. The margin is 2k/‖W‖. You can fix k = 1 without loss of generality — scaling W and k together does not move the boundary — and then the margin is 2/‖W‖. Making that large means making ‖W‖ small . Minimising ½‖W‖² instead of ‖W‖ changes nothing about where the minimum is and makes the derivative clean. So "widest street" and "smallest weights subject to getting everything right" are the same request. Notice what that means: the SVM's objective is a regularised one by construction. ½‖W‖² is the same L2 penalty from Module 4. Maximising the margin and shrinking the weights are the same act. Soft margin: allowing some mistakes Real data overlaps. Give every point a slack δᵢ ≥ 0 ("grace marks") and charge for it: Soft-margin SVM minimise  ½‖W‖² + C Σᵢ δᵢ     s.t.  yᵢ(W·Xᵢ) + δᵢ ≥ k
δ = 0         correct and outside the street
0 < δ < k     correct side, but inside the street
δ > k         misclassified
hinge loss:  max(0, 1 − y·f(x))  is exactly that slack The last line is the bridge to everything else in the course. Hinge loss is zero for a point that is correct and comfortably outside the margin, and grows linearly once it strays inside. So the soft-margin SVM is just hinge loss plus an L2 penalty — the same two-part recipe as Ridge regression, with a different loss. C Behaviour Risk Large (e.g. 1000+) Hates slack → narrow street, near "hard margin" Overfits, chases outliers (high variance) Small (e.g. 0.1–1) Tolerates slack → wide street Can underfit (higher bias)  C = how Cranky the teacher is about mistakes. C multiplies the total slack, so a large C makes each violation expensive and the model will narrow the street rather than pay for one. interactive lab svm  Support vectors The solution has the form W = Σ αᵢ yᵢ Xᵢ . For most points αᵢ = 0. It's non-zero only for points on the margin, inside it, or misclassified. Those are the support vectors ; delete every other training point and the boundary doesn't move. Prediction needs only them: y = sign(Σ αᵢ yᵢ (Xᵢ · X_test)), a dot product of the test point with each support vector. Two consequences worth holding onto. First, an SVM is non-parametric in the sense of Module 3 — it keeps training examples, and how many depends on the data. Second, that prediction formula contains the test point only inside a dot product with training points. Replace that dot product with something else and you get the kernel trick, which is the next chapter. LinearSVC defaults to squared hinge loss. To get the lecture's formulation you must pass loss='hinge' explicitly. At large C also pass max_iter=100000 or you will get convergence warnings. Assignment-1 Part 3 checks both of those. LinearSVC(C=1, loss='hinge') — the loss argument is rubric-checked. The 7-mark questions want the boundary and both margins drawn: with two features, solve w₀x₀ + w₁x₁ + b = c for x₁, giving x₁ = −(w₀x₀ + b − c) / w₁ for c = 0 (boundary), +1 and −1 (margins). Get w = svc.coef_[0] and b = svc.intercept_[0] . fit, measure the margin, draw all three lines import numpy as np, matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from sklearn.svm import LinearSVC

def run_linear_svc(X, y, C):
    svc = LinearSVC(C=C, loss="hinge", max_iter=100000).fit(X, y)
    w, b = svc.coef_[0], svc.intercept_[0]
    margin = 2 / np.linalg.norm(w)

    xs = np.linspace(X[:, 0].min(), X[:, 0].max(), 2)
    for c, style in [(0, "-"), (1, "--"), (-1, "--")]:
        plt.plot(xs, -(w[0] * xs + b - c) / w[1], style, color="k")
    plt.scatter(X[y == 0, 0], X[y == 0, 1], color="blue")
    plt.scatter(X[y == 1, 0], X[y == 1, 1], color="red")
    plt.title(f"C={C}  margin width {margin:.3f}")
    plt.show()
    return svc, margin

svc1,   m1   = run_linear_svc(X2, y2, C=1)      # margin 0.639
svc1000, m2  = run_linear_svc(X2, y2, C=1000)   # margin 0.243 Three lines from one formula, with c stepping through 0, +1 and −1. That is the whole of the 7-mark plotting question.

docs.text: Not scaling. The margin is measured in feature units, so an unscaled large column dominates ‖W‖ and the street is drawn almost entirely in that one direction. For SVMs, scaling is not a nicety. Expecting probabilities. An SVM returns a signed distance, not a probability. probability=True on SVC fits a separate calibration and is slow; logistic regression is usually the better choice if you need probabilities. Forgetting loss='hinge' . The silent default is squared hinge, which penalises violations quadratically and gives different margins. Large C on noisy data. The model will contort the boundary to accommodate one mislabelled point. That is the overfitting mode the dartboard chapter formalises. Too many rows. Kernel SVMs scale badly past tens of thousands of rows. LinearSVC handles large n; SVC does not. ISLP Ch 9 ISLP chapter 9 derives the maximal margin classifier, the support vector classifier (the soft-margin version) and support vector machines in sequence, with the same C-as-budget intuition and the same observation that only the support vectors matter.

Read this result carefully, because it is a good lesson in what an experiment does and does not show. The margin narrowed by a factor of 2.6 when C went up by a factor of 1,000 — exactly as the theory says. But accuracy stayed at 1.0 in both cases, because setosa and versicolor are easy and comfortably separable. So this experiment demonstrates the mechanism of C and tells you nothing about which C to choose. On easy data every reasonable setting wins. You find out whether C matters on hard data — which is the churn lab at the end of this module. dataset churn

docs.text: Reproduce Assignment Q11–Q15: keep iris classes 0 and 1, scatter them in two colours, split 80/20 with random_state=42 , fit LinearSVC(C=1, loss='hinge') , plot the boundary and both margins over the whole dataset, and report test accuracy. Success: margin 0.639, accuracy 1.0, three lines drawn. Repeat at C=1000. Success: margin 0.243, accuracy still 1.0, and you can explain why accuracy did not move. Identify the support vectors and confirm that deleting every other training point leaves the boundary unchanged. Success: refitting on only the support vectors gives the same coef_ to several decimals. Show the loss default matters: fit once with loss='hinge' and once without, and compare the margins. Success: they differ, and you can say which the rubric wants. Stretch goals Sweep C over six orders of magnitude and plot margin width against C on a log axis. The curve is the C knob made visible. Add one deliberately mislabelled point near the boundary and refit at C=1 and C=1000. Watch the large-C boundary distort to accommodate it while the small-C one ignores it. Implement hinge loss yourself and confirm that a point correct and outside the margin contributes exactly zero.

docs.chapterTitle: Margins, soft margins and support vectors
docs.moduleTitle: Linear classifiers, SVM, bias vs variance
docs.text: Pave the widest road: centre line is the boundary, kerbs are the margins, houses on the kerbs are the support vectors. Margin = 2/‖W‖, so maximising it means minimising ½‖W‖² — the same L2 penalty as Ridge. Soft-margin SVM = hinge loss + L2 penalty, with C weighting the slack. C = how Cranky about mistakes. Large C, narrow street, more variance. LinearSVC defaults to squared hinge — pass loss='hinge' explicitly. What happens to the margin as C increases? It narrows. A larger C makes each slack violation more expensive, so the model prefers a tighter street to paying for violations — approaching a hard margin, with more overfitting risk. Why does maximising the margin mean minimising ‖W‖? The total margin is 2k/‖W‖. Fixing k = 1 (a free choice, since scaling W and k together leaves the boundary unmoved) makes the margin 2/‖W‖, so a wider margin is a smaller ‖W‖. ½‖W‖² is used because its derivative is clean. Which points are the support vectors? Those with non-zero αᵢ — the points on the margin, inside it, or misclassified. Every other training point can be deleted without moving the boundary. Margin 0.639 at C=1 and 0.243 at C=1000, both with accuracy 1.0. What does that tell you? That C does what the theory says to the margin, and that this data is easy enough for accuracy not to distinguish the two. The mechanism is demonstrated; the choice of C is not.

docs.moduleTitle: Linear classifiers, SVM, bias vs variance
docs.text: Points on concentric rings can't be split by a line. Module 4's answer was polynomial features — add x², x₁x₂ and so on, and the linear model bends. That works, and on the breast-cancer data it was a disaster: degree 3 on 25 features produced thousands of columns and 75% test accuracy. The kernel trick gets the same expressive power without paying for those columns. That is the entire point, and it is one of the genuinely elegant ideas in machine learning.

docs.moduleTitle: Linear classifiers, SVM, bias vs variance
docs.text:
Points on concentric rings can't be split by a line. Map them with φ(x) = (x₁, x₂, x₁² + x₂²) and the inner ring sits low, the outer ring high: now a flat plane separates them. interactive lab kernel  Look at what the lab shows. The left panel never changes — lifting does not move the data. It adds a third reading of the same points, and in that reading a flat cut is enough. Back in the original two dimensions, that flat cut is a circle. Now recall the SVM's prediction from last chapter: y = sign(Σ αᵢ yᵢ (Xᵢ · X_test)) . The test point appears only inside a dot product with training points. So if you want to work in the lifted space, you do not need φ(x) itself — you only need φ(Xᵢ) · φ(X_test). And for many useful φ, that dot product has a closed form you can compute directly from the original coordinates. Kernelised SVM y = sign( Σ αᵢ yᵢ φ(Xᵢ)·φ(X_test) ) = sign( Σ αᵢ yᵢ K(Xᵢ, X_test) )
the kernel K computes the high-dimensional dot product without ever building φ That is the trick, stated plainly: you never build the new features. The RBF kernel corresponds to an infinite -dimensional φ, which you obviously could not construct — and computing exp(−γ‖a − b‖²) takes a subtraction, a norm and an exponential. Kernel K(a, b) Good for Linear a·b Many features, text, already separable Polynomial (a·b + c)^d Interactions between features RBF / Gaussian exp(−γ‖a − b‖²) Default for curved boundaries  The trick, verified with real numbers (polynomial kernel) Take a = (1, 2) and b = (3, 1) and the degree-2 kernel K(a, b) = (a · b)². • The shortcut: a · b = 1·3 + 2·1 = 5, so K = 5² = 25 . One dot product and one square. • The long way: the lift for this kernel is φ(x) = (x₁², √2·x₁x₂, x₂²). So φ(a) = (1, 2√2, 4) and φ(b) = (9, 3√2, 1). Their dot product: 1·9 + (2√2)(3√2) + 4·1 = 9 + 12 + 4 = 25 . Same answer, without ever building the 3-D vectors. For degree 3 on 25 features the lift has thousands of dimensions; the shortcut is still one dot product and one power. The RBF kernel, from zero RBF stands for radial basis function : “radial” because it depends only on the distance between the two points, not on direction. Read its formula from the inside out: 1. ‖a − b‖² — the squared distance between the points (Module 2). 2. −γ · distance² — make it negative and scale it by γ. 3. exp(…) — e to that power. e⁰ = 1, and e to a large negative number is almost 0. So K = 1 when the points are identical and slides smoothly towards 0 as they move apart. It is a similarity score shaped like a bell curve centred on each training point — that is why it is also called the Gaussian kernel. Worked example: a = (1, 2), b = (2, 0) ‖a − b‖² = (1 − 2)² + (2 − 0)² = 1 + 4 = 5

γ = 0.1   K = exp(−0.5) = 0.607     still quite similar: wide bubbles
γ = 0.5   K = exp(−2.5) = 0.082     barely similar
γ = 1     K = exp(−5)   = 0.0067    strangers
γ = 2     K = exp(−10)  ≈ 0.00005   might as well be on different planets

“influence radius” where K drops to 0.5:  d = √(ln 2 / γ)   (γ = 1 → d = 0.83) Now the prediction f(x) = Σ αᵢ yᵢ K(xᵢ, x) + b reads in plain English: every support vector casts a vote for its own class, and the vote's strength is how similar it is to the new point . Near a cluster of red support vectors their votes dominate and f says red. Far from every training point all similarities are ~0 and f falls back to the bias. The boundary is where the red and blue votes balance. interactive lab rbf Slide γ up from the default of 2 on the rings. Each similarity bubble shrinks and the boundary breaks into islands wrapped around single points: at γ = 2 the lab scores 100% train / 93% test, at γ = 20 it is 100% / 78%, at γ = 200 only 100% / 57%. Then go to small γ and drop C to 0.1: the boundary flattens and the model underfits (78% / 60%). Why does RBF correspond to infinitely many features? Expand the square: ‖a − b‖² = ‖a‖² + ‖b‖² − 2a·b, so K(a, b) = e^(−γ‖a‖²) · e^(−γ‖b‖²) · e^(2γ a·b). The last factor's Taylor series is 1 + 2γ(a·b) + (2γ a·b)²/2! + (2γ a·b)³/3! + … — a polynomial kernel of degree 1, plus degree 2, plus degree 3, forever. Each degree is a lifted feature space, so the RBF kernel is a dot product in the combination of all of them: infinitely many features, evaluated with one exponential. γ (gamma) controls how fast similarity fades with distance. Small γ: each point influences far away, smooth boundary (higher bias). Large γ: influence is local, wiggly boundary that can wrap single points (higher variance). You can also design your own kernels, or combine several (multiple kernel learning). Kernel = similarity score. "How alike are these two points?" The SVM votes using the similarity to each support vector. Read the RBF formula that way and it stops being opaque: ‖a − b‖² is the squared distance, the minus and the exponential turn distance into closeness, and γ sets how quickly closeness decays. The two knobs interact, which is why they are always tuned together. C controls how much the model cares about violations; γ controls how local the boundary can be. Large C with large γ is a model that will wrap itself around every individual training point — the highest-variance configuration available, and the one that produced a 0.40 train/test gap in the churn lab. the same problem, three kernels from sklearn.datasets import make_circles
from sklearn.svm import SVC
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split

X, y = make_circles(n_samples=400, noise=0.08, factor=0.4, random_state=42)
Xtr, Xte, ytr, yte = train_test_split(X, y, test_size=0.3, random_state=42)

for name, svc in [("linear", SVC(kernel="linear")),
                  ("poly d=2", SVC(kernel="poly", degree=2)),
                  ("rbf", SVC(kernel="rbf", gamma="scale"))]:
    svc.fit(Xtr, ytr)
    print(f"{name:<9} train {svc.score(Xtr, ytr):.3f}  test {svc.score(Xte, yte):.3f}  "
          f"support vectors {svc.n_support_.sum()}")

# What gamma does, holding C fixed
for g in [0.01, 0.1, 1, 10, 100]:
    s = SVC(kernel="rbf", C=1, gamma=g).fit(Xtr, ytr)
    print(f"gamma={g:<6} train {s.score(Xtr, ytr):.3f}  test {s.score(Xte, yte):.3f}  "
          f"SVs {s.n_support_.sum()}") Watch the support-vector count in the second loop. As gamma rises the model needs more and more of the training set to describe its boundary — which is what 'memorising' looks like from the inside.

docs.text: Not scaling. RBF is a function of ‖a − b‖², so an unscaled large-magnitude column decides every distance and γ becomes meaningless. This is the single most common reason an RBF SVM underperforms. Large γ with large C. Maximum variance. The model wraps individual points, training accuracy approaches 1.0 and test accuracy collapses. Reaching for RBF by default on wide data. With many features and few rows the data is usually already linearly separable, and a linear kernel is both faster and better. Text classification is the standard example. Too many rows. Kernel SVMs are roughly quadratic in n. Past tens of thousands of rows, use LinearSVC or an approximation like Nystroem . Tuning C and γ separately. They interact; grid-search them together. ISLP Ch 9 ISLP chapter 9 presents the kernel as an inner product in an enlarged space and makes the computational argument explicitly — that a kernel evaluates the enlarged inner product for every pair without ever working in the enlarged space.

docs.text: dataset churn Setting Train F1 Test F1 Gap Hard margin, linear 0.50 0.49 0.01 Hard margin, RBF 0.90 0.50 0.40 ← memorising Soft margin (C=1), linear 0.60 0.58 0.02 Soft margin (C=1), RBF 0.65 0.60 0.05 From the Telco churn notebook, F1 on the churn class. Row 2 is the whole cautionary tale. A hard-margin RBF — effectively C = ∞ with a flexible kernel — reaches 0.90 on training data and 0.50 on test. It has learnt the training set and nothing about churn. Row 4 is the same kernel with C = 1, and the gap drops from 0.40 to 0.05 while test F1 rises from 0.50 to 0.60. The flexibility was never the problem. The absence of a budget was.

docs.moduleTitle: Linear classifiers, SVM, bias vs variance
docs.text: Generate make_circles data and fit linear, polynomial and RBF kernels. Success: linear sits near 50%, the other two near 100%, and you can say why. Implement the lecture's lift by hand — add a third column x₁² + x₂² and fit a linear SVM in 3D. Success: it matches the RBF result, demonstrating that the kernel is a shortcut rather than a different idea. Sweep γ over five orders of magnitude at fixed C and record train accuracy, test accuracy and support-vector count. Success: you can identify the overfitting regime from the SV count alone. On the churn data, reproduce the four rows of the table above. Success: your hard-margin RBF shows a gap above 0.3. Stretch goals Verify the kernel identity numerically: compute (a·b + 1)² and compare it with the explicit dot product of the degree-2 polynomial feature maps of a and b. They should agree exactly — that equality is the trick. Grid-search C and γ together on churn with scoring="f1" and plot the result as a heatmap. The diagonal ridge you see is the C–γ interaction. Compare an RBF SVM against Nystroem + LinearSVC on the full 7,043-row churn data and compare both accuracy and fit time.

docs.moduleTitle: Linear classifiers, SVM, bias vs variance
docs.text: Kernel = similarity score. How alike are these two points? The test point appears only inside a dot product, so you never need φ itself. RBF corresponds to an infinite-dimensional lift and costs one exponential. Small γ = smooth and biased. Large γ = local and jumpy. Hard-margin RBF on real data is the clearest overfitting you will see: 0.90 train, 0.50 test. What exactly is the kernel trick? The SVM's prediction depends on the data only through dot products between points. A kernel computes the dot product in a higher-dimensional feature space directly from the original coordinates, so the lifted features are never constructed. Which points have non-zero α? Only the support vectors — the points on the margin, inside it, or misclassified. Everything else can be deleted without moving the boundary. What does gamma control in an RBF kernel? How quickly similarity decays with distance. Small gamma means wide influence and a smooth, higher-bias boundary; large gamma means local influence and a wiggly, higher-variance one. Train F1 0.90, test F1 0.50 on an RBF SVM. Diagnose it. A hard margin with a flexible kernel: the model has memorised the training set. Lower C to buy a slack budget — on churn that closed the gap from 0.40 to 0.05 and raised test F1.

docs.sectionTitle: Why one number cannot tell you what is wrong
docs.moduleTitle: Linear classifiers, SVM, bias vs variance
docs.text: Your model scores 72%. That number does not tell you what to do next, and the two possible problems need opposite fixes. If the model is consistently wrong — it would give nearly the same wrong answer however you resampled the training data — then the model family cannot express the pattern and you need more complexity. If the model is wrong differently every time — right on average but unstable — then it is fitting noise and you need less complexity, or more data, or an ensemble. Bias and variance are the names of those two failures, and telling them apart is the most practically useful diagnostic in the course.

docs.moduleTitle: Linear classifiers, SVM, bias vs variance
docs.text: Each dart is one model trained on a different sample, all predicting the same point. The bullseye is the truth. Tight cluster off-centre is bias; scattered around the centre is variance. interactive lab darts

docs.moduleTitle: Linear classifiers, SVM, bias vs variance
docs.text:
Imagine training the same kind of model on many different training sets D₁…D_M and predicting the same point X. Let g(X) be the average prediction. Definitions Bias(X)     = Y − g(X)                     (how far the average guess is from truth)
Variance(X) = (1/M) Σₘ (fₘ(X) − g(X))²      (how much the guesses disagree)
Expected error ≈ Bias² + Variance  (+ irreducible noise) Notice what each definition does and does not need. Bias compares the average prediction with the truth, so you need to know the truth. Variance compares the predictions with each other, so you do not. That asymmetry is why variance is the one you can actually estimate in practice — resample, refit, and look at the spread — while bias generally has to be inferred from the train/test gap. The third line is the decomposition that matters. Total error splits into a part from being systematically off, a part from being unstable, and a part that is irreducible — the noise in the data itself, which no model can remove. Chasing zero error is chasing that third term, which is why a perfect score should make you suspicious rather than pleased.  Low variance High variance Low bias Ideal Overfitting: right on average, unstable High bias Underfitting: consistently wrong Worst of both  High Bias = Blind to the pattern (underfit). High Variance = Very jumpy (overfit).  The lecture's worked example X = [3, 5], Y = 12, four datasets. Predictions 11.3, 11.3, 14.7, 11.3 → mean 12.15. Bias = 12 − 12.15 = −0.15 (tiny). Squared deviations 0.7225, 0.7225, 6.5025, 0.7225 → variance 2.17. Low bias, modest variance. If the truth were Y = 18 with the same predictions, the models agree as much as before (variance still 2.17) but they're all far off: high bias . The model family is wrong for the data. That second half is the cleanest demonstration of the independence of the two quantities. Nothing about the models changed — the same four predictions, the same disagreement among them. Only the truth moved. Variance is a property of the estimator ; bias is a property of the estimator relative to the truth . The slide lists the Y = 18 bias as 1.35. Recomputing: errors are 6.7, 6.7, 3.3, 6.7, mean 5.85, and 18 − 12.15 = 5.85. Also, the variance formula on the slide is printed as (1/M)·(Y − g(X))²; the intended one is (1/M)·Σ(fₘ(X) − g(X))², which is what the table computes. Which knob moves which Change Bias Variance More model complexity (degree, depth, γ, C) ↓ ↑ Stronger regularisation (α up, C down) ↑ ↓ More training data — ↓ Bagging / random forest — ↓↓ Boosting ↓↓ ↑ (mildly) Better features ↓ — Note the asymmetry: more data reduces variance and does nothing for bias. If your model is underfitting, collecting more rows will not help.

docs.sectionTitle: How to diagnose it in practice
docs.moduleTitle: Linear classifiers, SVM, bias vs variance
docs.text: You cannot usually train on many datasets, so you infer the decomposition from two numbers you do have. Train score Test score Diagnosis Do Low Low Underfitting (high bias) More features, more complex model, less regularisation High Much lower Overfitting (high variance) More data, regularise, simpler model, bagging, feature selection High Close to train Good fit Tune threshold, ship  Do not diagnose from the test score alone. 72% test could be either row. You need the gap. Do not add data to fix bias. It will not move. Add features or capacity instead. Do not add capacity to fix variance. That is the direction that caused it. Beware the irreducible floor. If two very different model families both plateau at the same score, you may be at the noise limit and further tuning is wasted effort. Estimate variance directly when you can. Refit on several bootstrap resamples and look at the spread of predictions for a fixed row — that is the dartboard, computed. ISLP Ch 2 ISLP chapter 2 derives the expected test MSE decomposition into variance, squared bias and irreducible error, and shows the characteristic U-shaped test-error curve against flexibility that this chapter's trade-off produces.

docs.moduleTitle: Linear classifiers, SVM, bias vs variance
docs.text:
dataset churn Model Train Test Gap Reading Linear, degree 1 (breast cancer) 95.8% 98.2% −2.4 No overfitting at all Linear, degree 3 (breast cancer) 100.0% 75.4% 24.6 High variance Ridge α=10⁴, degree 3 90.5% 90.4% 0.1 High bias — over-regularised Hard-margin RBF SVM (churn F1) 0.90 0.50 0.40 High variance Soft-margin linear SVM (churn F1) 0.60 0.58 0.02 Balanced, modest capacity Every one of these is a real result from the course notebooks. The Reading column is the diagnosis the gap supports. Row 3 is the one students usually misread. A gap of 0.1 looks excellent, and the model is still bad — both numbers are 8 points below what a plain degree-1 fit achieved. A small gap means low variance, not a good model. You need both halves: a small gap and a high level. estimating variance by resampling import numpy as np
from sklearn.linear_model import LinearRegression
from sklearn.utils import resample

rng = np.random.default_rng(42)
row = X_test.iloc[[0]]                      # one fixed point to predict
preds = []
for _ in range(60):
    Xb, yb = resample(X_train, y_train, random_state=rng.integers(1e6))
    preds.append(LinearRegression().fit(Xb, yb).predict(row)[0])

preds = np.array(preds)
print("mean prediction g(X):", preds.mean().round(4))
print("variance            :", preds.var().round(4))
print("spread (min..max)   :", preds.min().round(3), "..", preds.max().round(3)) This is the dartboard, computed on real data: 60 models trained on 60 resamples, all predicting one patient. The spread is the variance you have been reading about.
