docs.text: Reproduce the lecture's worked example by hand: predictions 11.3, 11.3, 14.7, 11.3 against Y = 12. Success: mean 12.15, bias −0.15, variance 2.17. Redo it with Y = 18 and confirm the corrected bias. Success: 5.85, not the slide's 1.35, and you can show why. Run the resampling code above and report g(X) and the variance for one test patient. Success: you have a real number for variance, not an intuition. Classify each of the five rows in the results table into a quadrant. Success: you put Ridge α=10⁴ in the high-bias box despite its tiny gap. Stretch goals Plot a full bias–variance curve: for polynomial degrees 1 to 10, resample 40 times each, and plot estimated squared bias, variance and total test error on one set of axes. The U-shape in the total is the trade-off. Repeat the resampling experiment with a deep decision tree instead of linear regression. The variance should be dramatically larger — which is exactly the setup bagging exists to fix, in the next module.

docs.moduleTitle: Linear classifiers, SVM, bias vs variance
docs.text: High Bias = Blind to the pattern. High Variance = Very jumpy. Bias needs the truth; variance only needs the models to disagree — which is why variance is measurable. Error = bias² + variance + irreducible noise. The third term is why a perfect score is suspicious. More data reduces variance and does nothing for bias. A small train/test gap is not a good model — Ridge at α=10⁴ had a 0.1 gap and was 8 points worse. Define bias and variance in this setting. Train the same model family on many different training sets and predict one point. Bias is the gap between the truth and the average prediction; variance is how much the individual predictions disagree with that average. A model scores 72% on test. Is it high bias or high variance? Unanswerable from that alone. You need the training score: low train and low test is high bias, high train and much lower test is high variance. Would more data fix underfitting? No. More data reduces variance, not bias. Underfitting needs more capacity or better features. In the lecture example with Y = 18, what is the bias? 5.85 — the mean prediction is 12.15 and 18 − 12.15 = 5.85. The slide's 1.35 is an arithmetic error; the variance is unchanged at 2.17 because the predictions did not move.

docs.chapterTitle: Class imbalance, and the churn notebook
docs.sectionTitle: Why the same error count can be two different models
docs.moduleTitle: Linear classifiers, SVM, bias vs variance
docs.text: Lecture example: 12 blue, 5 red. Two classifiers each make 3 mistakes. Classifier 1 gets 0/12 blue wrong but 3/5 red wrong — 60% of the minority class . Classifier 2 gets 3/12 blue wrong and 0/5 red wrong. Both have the same total error. A training algorithm minimising total error may pick either, with no preference. The second is obviously fairer and more useful, and nothing in the loss function knows that. Telco churn: ~27% leave. A model that says "nobody leaves" is 73% accurate and useless. Judge on recall and F1 for the churn class, and train with balanced weights. The minority class is almost always the one you care about. Fraud, churn, disease, equipment failure, security incidents — in every case the rare event is the reason the project exists. Imbalance is not an edge case; it is the normal condition of useful classification problems.

docs.chapterTitle: Class imbalance, and the churn notebook
docs.moduleTitle: Linear classifiers, SVM, bias vs variance
docs.text:
Fix How Note Oversample minority Add more minority examples: inexact copies close in feature space SMOTE does exactly this, interpolating between neighbours Undersample majority Drop majority examples, preferably near the boundary Throws away data; fine when data is plentiful Class weights Make each minority mistake cost more class_weight="balanced" : w_c = n / (k × n_c)  Take the weight formula apart, because it is used unchanged in the next module. With n rows, k classes and n_c rows in class c, the weight is n / (k · n_c). For a 73/27 split with 1,000 rows: the majority weight is 1000/(2·730) = 0.68 and the minority weight is 1000/(2·270) = 1.85. Multiply each class's count by its weight and both come to 500 — the weights are exactly what makes the effective class counts equal. Balanced weights do not change the data — they change the price of each mistake. Which is why they are usually the first thing to try: no rows invented, no rows discarded, one argument. Which to pick, in practice. Class weights first: one argument, no data distortion, works for SVMs, logistic regression and trees. Oversampling / SMOTE when the minority is very small and the model needs more examples to shape a boundary — but it must happen inside the cross-validation fold, or synthetic points derived from a validation row end up in training. Undersampling only when you have data to spare. And independently of all three: move the threshold . A probabilistic model trained on imbalanced data can often be fixed at prediction time rather than training time, which is cheaper and more controllable. The threshold lab from Module 3 is the tool. The churn workflow Load 7,043 customers; TotalCharges is text → pd.to_numeric(errors="coerce") ; the 11 NaNs are tenure-0 customers, so drop them. EDA: churners are new, pay more per month, sit on month-to-month contracts, fibre internet, electronic cheque. Drop customerID , target Yes→1, pd.get_dummies(drop_first=True) , stratified split. Scale numeric columns : w·x adds features, so TotalCharges (thousands) would drown tenure (tens). Compare hard/soft margin × linear/RBF, then tune C and γ with GridSearchCV inside a Pipeline. Step 1 is a good reminder that data cleaning is domain reasoning, not mechanics. TotalCharges is blank for exactly the customers whose tenure is 0 — they have been billed nothing because they have been there no months. The 11 NaNs are not errors; they are a category. Dropping them is defensible because they cannot have churned yet. Put the scaler inside the Pipeline when cross-validating. Otherwise it's fit on all training folds, including the one being used for validation: leakage. the whole churn pipeline, leak-free import pandas as pd
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split, GridSearchCV, StratifiedKFold
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler
from sklearn.compose import ColumnTransformer
from sklearn.pipeline import Pipeline
from sklearn.svm import SVC
from sklearn.metrics import classification_report

url = "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/IBM/telco-customer-churn-on-icp4d/master/data/Telco-Customer-Churn.csv"
df = pd.read_csv(url)            # or the offline practice file: churn_practice_synthetic.csv
df["TotalCharges"] = pd.to_numeric(df["TotalCharges"], errors="coerce")
df = df.dropna(subset=["TotalCharges"]).drop(columns="customerID")
y = (df.pop("Churn") == "Yes").astype(int)
X = pd.get_dummies(df, drop_first=True, dtype=int)
num = ["tenure", "MonthlyCharges", "TotalCharges"]
X_tr, X_te, y_tr, y_te = train_test_split(X, y, test_size=0.2, stratify=y, random_state=42)

pipe = Pipeline([
    ("scale", ColumnTransformer([("s", StandardScaler(), num)], remainder="passthrough")),
    ("svm", SVC(kernel="rbf", class_weight="balanced", random_state=42)),
])
grid = GridSearchCV(pipe,
    {"svm__C": [0.1, 1, 10, 100], "svm__gamma": [0.001, 0.01, 0.1, 1]},
    cv=StratifiedKFold(5, shuffle=True, random_state=42),
    scoring="f1", return_train_score=True, n_jobs=-1)
grid.fit(X_tr, y_tr)
print(grid.best_params_, round(grid.best_score_, 3))
print(classification_report(y_te, grid.best_estimator_.predict(X_te)))

res = pd.DataFrame(grid.cv_results_)[["param_svm__C", "param_svm__gamma", "mean_train_score", "mean_test_score"]]
res["gap"] = res.mean_train_score - res.mean_test_score     # big gap = high variance
print(res.sort_values("gap", ascending=False).round(3)) Four things to copy: ColumnTransformer scales only the numeric columns and passes the one-hot ones through; class_weight='balanced' prices the minority correctly; scoring='f1' optimises the thing you actually care about; and return_train_score gives you the gap column that diagnoses every cell of the grid. That last block — sorting the grid by train-minus-test gap — is the most reusable idea in the notebook. It turns a hyperparameter search into a bias–variance map: the cells with the biggest gaps are the high-variance corner (large C, large γ), and the cells with low scores on both are the underfitting corner.

docs.moduleTitle: Linear classifiers, SVM, bias vs variance
docs.text: Reporting accuracy. On 27% churn, "nobody leaves" scores 73%. Always print the majority baseline beside your number. Resampling outside the fold. SMOTE or oversampling applied before cross-validation leaks: synthetic points built from a validation row train the model that is then validated on it. Use imblearn 's Pipeline, which resamples per fold. Scaling outside the Pipeline. Same class of error, and the one the lecture flags explicitly. One-hot encoding before splitting. Usually harmless, but if a category appears only in test you get a column mismatch. Encode inside the Pipeline or align the columns explicitly. Balancing when you do not need to. If the costs really are symmetric and the classes are only mildly unequal, weighting shifts the threshold for no benefit. drop_first=True with a model that has no intercept. It avoids the dummy-variable trap for linear models; for trees it just removes information. ISLP Ch 9 ISLP chapter 9 covers the SVM with unequal class costs and the ROC curve as the summary of a classifier across all thresholds — the right way to compare two models when the operating point is still undecided.

docs.text: dataset churn Setting Train F1 Test F1 Gap Hard margin, linear 0.50 0.49 0.01 Hard margin, RBF 0.90 0.50 0.40 ← memorising Soft margin (C=1), linear 0.60 0.58 0.02 Soft margin (C=1), RBF 0.65 0.60 0.05  Read the F1 values rather than the gaps for a moment. The best test F1 here is 0.60 — which is not a great model, and that is the honest result for churn from these features. Churn is genuinely hard: people leave for reasons that are not in a billing table. A 0.60 F1 that you understand is worth more than a 0.90 accuracy that you have misread. Use it when you cannot reach the IBM URL; the real file has 7,043 rows.

docs.moduleTitle: Linear classifiers, SVM, bias vs variance
docs.text: Equal total error can hide a 60% failure rate on the minority class. Balanced weights change the price of a mistake, not the data: w_c = n / (k · n_c). Resampling and scaling both belong inside the cross-validation fold. Sort a hyperparameter grid by train-minus-test gap and it becomes a bias–variance map. The honest churn result is F1 ≈ 0.60, and understanding that beats misreading 73% accuracy. Two classifiers make three mistakes each on 12 blue and 5 red. Are they equally good? No. One gets 3 of the 5 red wrong — 60% of the minority — while the other gets all the red right. Total error treats them identically, which is why you report per-class recall. What does class_weight='balanced' actually compute? w_c = n / (k · n_c), so each class's weighted count becomes n/k. For a 73/27 split the weights are about 0.68 and 1.85, making the effective class sizes equal. Why must the scaler sit inside the Pipeline during cross-validation? Fitted outside, it has seen every training fold including the one being held out for validation, so the validation score is contaminated. A Pipeline refits it per fold. A churn model is 73% accurate. What do you ask next? What the majority baseline scores — also 73% — and what the recall on the churn class is. If recall is near zero the model has learnt nothing useful.

docs.chapterTitle: Discriminative features, entropy and information gain
docs.sectionTitle: Why some questions are worth asking
docs.text: A decision tree asks the one question that best separates the classes, then asks again inside each answer. An ensemble asks many trees and takes the vote. Number of legs can't separate cats from dogs: every example has the same value. Colour overlaps too much. A discriminative feature has different label distributions for its different values. House colour barely predicts price; location does. "Different label distributions for different values" is the whole criterion, and the rest of this chapter is about how to put a number on it — because a tree has to compare candidate questions automatically, and "looks more separated" is not something an algorithm can act on.

docs.chapterTitle: Discriminative features, entropy and information gain
docs.text:
Lecture example: one shopper rated 100 cameras. Group ratings into LOW (1–3) and HIGH (4–5). 63 LOW, 37 HIGH overall. Split Group LOW HIGH P(HIGH | group) Verdict Company C1 43 11 0.20 Good: groups differ a lot Company C2 20 26 0.55 Good: groups differ a lot Price < 300 yes 45 25 0.36 Bad: groups look alike Price < 300 no 18 12 0.40 Bad: groups look alike Price < 500 yes 55 35 0.40 Doubtful: one group has only 10 cameras Price < 500 no 8 2 0.20 Doubtful: one group has only 10 cameras  Read the P(HIGH) column. Company splits 100 cameras into groups where the chance of a HIGH rating is 0.20 and 0.55 — a real difference. Price < 300 gives 0.36 and 0.40, which is almost no difference at all. Price < 500 looks like a difference (0.40 versus 0.20) but one side has only 10 cameras, so that 0.20 is two cameras out of ten and could easily be noise. Those three verdicts are exactly what information gain will compute, and the third one shows why the formula weights children by size . Entropy Entropy of a group H = − Σ pᵢ log pᵢ
50/50 → maximum uncertainty (1 bit with log₂, 0.69 with ln)
90/10 → low uncertainty (0.47 bits, 0.33 with ln)
pure  → 0 Entropy = how surprised you'd be pulling a marble from the bag. Information gain = how much less surprised you are after the split. A 50/50 bag is maximum surprise — you genuinely cannot guess. A pure bag is zero surprise — you always know. Information gain of a split IG = H(parent) − Σ (size of child / size of parent) × H(child)
Company:     0.66 − (0.54 × 0.51 + 0.46 × 0.68) ≈ 0.07   ← winner
Price<300:   0.66 − (0.70 × 0.65 + 0.30 × 0.67) ≈ 0
Price<500:   0.66 − (0.90 × 0.67 + 0.10 × 0.50) ≈ 0.01 The size weighting is what demotes Price < 500. Its small child is genuinely purer (H = 0.50), but it holds only 10% of the cameras, so it contributes 0.10 × 0.50 to the weighted average and barely moves the total. A split that purifies a tiny corner of the data has not told you much about the data. The slide numbers (0.66 for the 63/37 root) use the natural log. sklearn's criterion="entropy" uses log₂, which gives 0.95 for the same root. The base only rescales every number by the same factor, so the ranking of splits, and the tree, stays identical. interactive lab entropy  Gini impurity (sklearn's default) Gini G = 1 − Σ pᵢ²     "chance a random guess from the bag's own mix is wrong"
10/0 → 0     8/2 → 0.32     5/5 → 0.50   (entropy: 0, 0.72, 1.00 bits) Gini and entropy almost always pick the same split. Gini is slightly cheaper (no logarithm). The quoted interpretation is worth unpacking because it makes Gini memorable: draw a marble at random, then guess its colour by drawing a second marble at random from the same bag. The chance you guess wrong is 1 − Σpᵢ². For a pure bag it is zero; for 50/50 it is a half. reproducing the lecture's three numbers import pandas as pd, numpy as np

df = pd.read_csv("camera_ratings_lecture.csv")
print(pd.crosstab(df.company, df.rating_band, margins=True))
print(pd.crosstab(df.price_usd < 300, df.rating_band, margins=True))
print(pd.crosstab(df.price_usd < 500, df.rating_band, margins=True))

def entropy(labels):
    p = labels.value_counts(normalize=True)
    return -(p * np.log(p)).sum()          # natural log, like the slides

def info_gain(df, mask, target="rating_band"):
    n = len(df); left, right = df[mask], df[~mask]
    return entropy(df[target]) - (len(left)/n*entropy(left[target]) + len(right)/n*entropy(right[target]))

print("Company   IG", round(info_gain(df, df.company == "C1"), 3))
print("Price<300 IG", round(info_gain(df, df.price_usd < 300), 3))
print("Price<500 IG", round(info_gain(df, df.price_usd < 500), 3)) Swap np.log for np.log2 and every number scales by 1/ln(2) ≈ 1.443 — the root goes 0.66 → 0.95 and the gains 0.07 → 0.10 — while the ranking is untouched.

docs.chapterTitle: Discriminative features, entropy and information gain
docs.text: Information gain favours many-valued features. A feature with a unique value per row (an ID, a timestamp) splits the data into pure singletons and scores maximum gain while predicting nothing. Gain ratio, or simply dropping ID-like columns, is the fix. Comparing gains across log bases. 0.07 nats and 0.10 bits are the same split. Never compare a number from the slides with one from sklearn without converting. Reading a small gain as a useless feature. The camera winner scores only 0.07, and it is still the best question available. Gains are relative to the candidates, not absolute. Forgetting the size weighting. Purifying 10% of the data is not the same as purifying half of it. Expecting entropy to notice interactions. Each split is scored on its own. A pair of features that are useless alone and perfect together will not be found by greedy single-feature gain. ISLP Ch 8 ISLP chapter 8 covers the classification error rate, Gini and entropy as the three node-impurity measures, and explains why Gini and entropy are preferred for growing the tree while classification error is preferred for pruning it.

docs.text: dataset camera Candidate split IG (nats) IG (bits) Verdict Company (C1 vs C2) 0.07 0.10 Winner — the tree's first question Price < 300 ≈ 0.00 ≈ 0.00 Tells you nothing Price < 500 ≈ 0.01 ≈ 0.01 Doubtful — one child has 10 rows The professor rebuilt this 100-row file so its counts match the lecture slides exactly, which means these three numbers are reproducible to the decimal. docs.chapterTitle: Discriminative features, entropy and information gain
docs.text: Reproduce the three crosstabs and confirm they match the lecture counts: C1 43/11, C2 20/26, price<300 45/25 and 18/12, price<500 55/35 and 8/2. Success: exact match. Compute the three information gains in nats. Success: 0.07, ≈0, ≈0.01 — the slide's numbers. Recompute in bits and confirm the ranking is unchanged. Success: root entropy 0.95, and you can state the conversion factor. Compute entropy and Gini for 10/0, 8/2 and 5/5 by hand. Success: Gini 0, 0.32, 0.50 and entropy 0, 0.72, 1.00 bits. Stretch goals Add a fake ID column with a unique value per camera and compute its information gain. It will be maximal and the feature is worthless — the clearest possible demonstration of why gain alone is not enough. Plot entropy against p for a two-class bag, from 0 to 1, and mark where it peaks. Then overlay Gini and see how closely the two curves track each other. Score every candidate split on the camera data — every feature, every threshold — and rank them. That ranking is exactly what a tree computes at its root.

docs.chapterTitle: Discriminative features, entropy and information gain
docs.text: A discriminative feature has different label distributions for different values. Entropy = how surprised you'd be. Information gain = how much less surprised after the split. IG weights each child by its size — purifying a tiny corner does not count for much. The slides use ln, sklearn uses log₂. Same ranking, different numbers. Gini is the chance a random guess from the bag's own mix is wrong. Entropy (log₂) of a group with 8 stay and 2 churn? About 0.72 bits. −(0.8·log₂0.8 + 0.2·log₂0.2) = 0.72. Its Gini is 1 − (0.64 + 0.04) = 0.32. What is information gain, in words? The parent's entropy minus the size-weighted average entropy of the children — how much uncertainty the split removed. The slides say the 63/37 root has entropy 0.66 but sklearn says 0.95. Who is wrong? Neither. The slides use the natural log and sklearn uses log₂; the ratio is 1/ln 2 ≈ 1.443. The base rescales every value equally, so the chosen split is identical. Why does a unique-ID feature score maximum information gain? It splits the data into pure single-row children, so the weighted child entropy is zero. The gain is maximal and the feature predicts nothing about new data — which is why gain ratio exists, and why ID columns get dropped.

docs.chapterTitle: Growing a tree, regression trees, multi-class and voting
docs.text: A single decision tree is rarely the most accurate model you can build. It is often the most useful , because it is the only model in this course whose reasoning a manager can read off a page: "C2 brand, under $500, predict HIGH". No coefficients, no scaling, no probability calibration — just nested questions. And it is the foundation of random forests and gradient boosting, which are the most accurate models for tabular data. Learning the tree is learning the building block.

docs.chapterTitle: Growing a tree, regression trees, multi-class and voting
docs.text:
Find the feature (and threshold) with maximum information gain. Split the data on it. For each child, check whether any further split gives information gain. If yes, split again; if no, stop and make it a leaf. Repeat from step 3. A leaf predicts the mode label of its training examples. Camera tree: root (63 L / 37 H) → C1 (43/11) and C2 (20/26) → then Price < 500 inside each. Test camera: Company C2, price 350 → C2 branch → price < 500 leaf (15 L / 25 H) → predict HIGH . A one-split tree is called a decision stump (69% training accuracy here). From zero: how “the best split” is scored A tree needs a number that says how mixed a group is. A bag of 10 blue marbles is perfectly pure; 5 blue + 5 red is as mixed as two classes can get. Two standard scores, where pₖ is the fraction of class k in the node: • Gini impurity = 1 − Σ pₖ². Reading: pick two items at random (with replacement); Gini is the chance they have different labels. Pure → 0, 50/50 → 0.5. • Entropy = −Σ pₖ log₂ pₖ. Reading: how many yes/no questions you need on average to guess the label. Pure → 0, 50/50 → 1 bit. Worked example: scoring the Company split on the 100 cameras root      63 LOW / 37 HIGH     Gini = 1 − (0.63² + 0.37²)           = 0.466
C1        43 / 11  (54 cams)   Gini = 1 − (43/54)² − (11/54)²        = 0.324
C2        20 / 26  (46 cams)   Gini = 1 − (20/46)² − (26/46)²        = 0.491

weighted child impurity = 0.54 × 0.324 + 0.46 × 0.491 = 0.401
Gini decrease (gain)    = 0.466 − 0.401                = 0.065

same split with entropy (log₂): root 0.951 → children 0.848 → gain 0.103 bits
(with natural log, as on the slides: 0.659 → gain ≈ 0.07) The algorithm computes this gain for every feature and every possible threshold — for a numeric column, every midpoint between consecutive sorted values — and keeps the single best. Then it repeats inside each child. That is the entire training procedure. Gini and entropy almost always choose the same split; Gini is a little faster because it has no logarithm, which is why it is sklearn's default. interactive lab treesplit Score splits yourself first: drag the threshold and watch the weighted impurity and the gain change, then press “Snap to best split”. Then switch to “Let the algorithm grow it” and raise the depth until every leaf is pure — and notice what that does to the boxes. Trace that prediction and notice what the model is actually doing: it has partitioned the feature space into rectangular boxes, and every point in a box gets the same answer. That is the tree's inductive bias — axis-aligned rectangles . A boundary at 45° has to be approximated by a staircase of them, which is why a tree struggles with exactly the data a linear model handles easily, and vice versa. Advantages Disadvantages Easy to read and explain; fast predictions; ranks features by usefulness; handles mixed and categorical features; no scaling needed Greedy heuristic, no optimal guarantee; a deep tree memorises (high variance); small data changes can reshape the whole tree  "Greedy" is doing real work in that sentence. The tree picks the best single split at each step and never reconsiders. There may be a worse first split that enables two excellent second splits, and the algorithm will never find it — searching all trees is NP-hard, so every practical tree is greedy. This is also why a tree cannot discover a pure interaction: neither feature in an XOR pair has any gain on its own. Control depth with max_depth , min_samples_split , min_samples_leaf , or prune afterwards ( ccp_alpha ). Regression trees Predicting the average rating (a real number)? Swap entropy for variance , information gain for variance reduction , and the leaf mode for the leaf mean . Variance reduction Company:       1.1 − (0.54 × 1.5 + 0.46 × 0.5) = 0.06
Video ≥ 30fps: 1.1 − (0.70 × 1.2 + 0.30 × 0.4) = 0.14   ← split on video rate Classification tree: entropy → gain → mode. Regression tree: variance → reduction → mean. Three substitutions and the same algorithm. Notice that the best split changed — Company won on the classification target, video rate wins on the numeric one. Multi-class with binary classifiers A single line splits space into two halves, so a linear classifier is binary. For K classes:  One-vs-one One-vs-all (rest) Train every pair of classes each class vs everyone else Number of models K(K − 1)/2 (3 classes → 3, 10 → 45) K Decide each model votes; most votes wins the class whose model says "yes" (most confidently)  One-vs-one is a round-robin tournament. One-vs-all is "you against the world".  The trade is between count and balance. One-vs-all trains only K models but each one faces a deliberately imbalanced problem — one class against K−1 of them. One-vs-one trains K(K−1)/2 models, which grows quadratically, but each is a small balanced two-class problem. For K = 3 the difference is 3 versus 3; for K = 10 it is 10 versus 45. A decision tree needs neither, because a leaf can hold any label. Voting Simple voting: classification takes the mode , regression the mean . Weighted voting gives reliable models more say (weights from validation accuracy). Model f1 f2 f3 f4 f5 f6 Predicted label 1 1 2 1 3 2 Weight 7 5 9 5 7 9  Simple vote: label 1 wins 3–2–1. Weighted: label 1 = 7 + 5 + 5 = 17, label 2 = 9 + 9 = 18, label 3 = 7 → label 2 wins. Weights can flip the decision. In the weighted regression example the slide multiplies f6 by 6 instead of its weight 9. With 9: (7.7 + 4.0 + 20.7 + 7.5 + 21.7 + 24.3) / 42 = 85.9 / 42 ≈ 2.05. The conclusion (≈ 2) holds either way. the camera tree, printed as rules import pandas as pd
from sklearn.tree import DecisionTreeClassifier, export_text

df = pd.read_csv("camera_ratings_lecture.csv")
X = pd.get_dummies(df[["company", "color", "resolution_mp", "video_fps", "price_usd"]],
                   drop_first=True)
tree = DecisionTreeClassifier(criterion="entropy", max_depth=2).fit(X, df.rating_band)
print(export_text(tree, feature_names=list(X.columns)))

# The lecture's test camera: C2, Black, 15 MP, 30 fps, $350
test = pd.DataFrame([{"company_C2": 1, "color_White": 0,
                      "resolution_mp": 15, "video_fps": 30, "price_usd": 350}])
print(tree.predict(test[X.columns]))          # -> HIGH

# A stump, for comparison
stump = DecisionTreeClassifier(criterion="entropy", max_depth=1).fit(X, df.rating_band)
print("stump training accuracy", stump.score(X, df.rating_band).round(3))   # ~0.69 `export_text` is the reason to reach for a tree at all — the model prints itself as readable rules, which no other model in this course can do.

docs.text: Unconstrained depth. A tree grown to purity memorises. Near-perfect train, weak test. Always set max_depth or min_samples_leaf , or prune. Instability. Change a few rows and the root split can change, reshaping the entire tree. Never present a single tree's structure as "the" explanation — the next module's forest exists partly because of this. Diagonal boundaries. Axis-aligned rectangles approximate a 45° line with a staircase, needing many splits for something a linear model does with two weights. Pure interactions. Greedy single-feature gain cannot find an XOR pair, because neither feature has any gain alone. Extrapolation. A regression tree's leaf predicts a mean, so it can never predict outside the range of its training targets. Linear models extrapolate; trees cannot. Reading feature importances as causes. They measure how much each feature reduced impurity in this fitted tree, and correlated features split the credit arbitrarily. ISLP Ch 8 ISLP chapter 8 builds regression trees first and classification trees second, covers cost-complexity pruning properly, and gives the clearest statement of trees-versus-linear-models: whichever one's assumption matches the true boundary wins.

docs.chapterTitle: Growing a tree, regression trees, multi-class and voting
docs.text: Find the best split, split, repeat, stop when no split gains anything; a leaf predicts the mode. A tree's inductive bias is axis-aligned rectangles — a staircase for a diagonal. Classification: entropy → gain → mode. Regression: variance → reduction → mean. One-vs-one is a round-robin, K(K−1)/2 models. One-vs-all is you against the world, K models. Weighted voting can flip the simple-majority answer: 18 beats 17. What does a leaf predict in a classification tree, and in a regression tree? The mode of its training labels for classification, the mean of its training targets for regression. The split criterion changes the same way: entropy/gain becomes variance/variance-reduction. How many models does one-vs-one need for 10 classes? K(K − 1)/2 = 45. One-vs-all needs only 10, but each faces an imbalanced one-against-nine problem. Why can a greedy tree not learn XOR? Neither feature has any information gain on its own, so the first split finds nothing to pick. The pattern only exists in the interaction, and greedy single-feature search never evaluates it. Why can a regression tree not extrapolate? Every leaf predicts the mean of its training targets, so no prediction can ever fall outside the range of the training labels. A linear model has no such limit.

docs.sectionTitle: Why a committee beats an expert
docs.text: A deep decision tree is a high-variance model: change a few training rows and the whole tree reshapes. The previous chapter listed that as a disadvantage. This chapter turns it into the engine of the best tabular models in use. The insight is that instability is only a problem for one tree. Train many trees that are each unstable in a different way, and their individual errors are partly random — so averaging cancels them. Bagging = a committee of slightly different experts. Each overfits in its own way, the vote cancels the quirks.

Why averaging helps The variance of an average Var((X₁ + X₂)/2) = ¼Var(X₁) + ¼Var(X₂) + ½Cov(X₁, X₂)

with zero covariance:  = ½ Var   → half the variance
with high covariance:  → barely any reduction at all That one line explains everything else in the chapter. Average K independent predictions and variance falls by a factor of K. But the covariance term does not vanish on its own, and if the models are similar it dominates — which is exactly what happens to bagged trees when one feature is overwhelmingly predictive, and exactly what random forests fix. Bootstrap But we only have one training set. Bootstrap : draw N rows with replacement from the N we have. Some rows appear twice or three times, others not at all. Repeat to get K different training sets, train a model on each, vote. interactive lab boot  The 36.8% rule P(a given row is never picked in N draws) = (1 − 1/N)ᴺ → 1/e ≈ 0.368
so each bootstrap sample leaves out ~1/3 of the rows: the "out-of-bag" (OOB) set,
a free validation set Derive it once and it stops being a magic number. One draw misses a given row with probability (1 − 1/N). N independent draws all miss it with probability (1 − 1/N)ᴺ, and that expression converges to 1/e as N grows. So roughly 36.8% of rows are left out of each bootstrap sample and 63.2% are included — which is the 10,449 / 16,512 = 63.3% the study guide measured. The practical payoff is the out-of-bag score. Each tree has a third of the data it never saw, so you can evaluate it on that third — and averaging over all trees gives a validation estimate without holding anything out. oob_score=True gets it for free. Random forest Bagged trees still look alike if one feature (contract type, tenure) dominates every split. Their errors correlate, so the ½Cov term keeps variance high. Random forest adds feature bagging : at each split, a tree may only look at a random subset of features (typically √p for classification). Trees disagree more, the vote cancels more noise. Method Randomises Mainly reduces Single deep tree nothing (high variance) Bagging rows variance Random forest rows + features at every split variance, more strongly Boosting (next: AdaBoost, Gradient Boosting, XGBoost) focuses on previous mistakes, trains sequentially bias  Bagging is a Parallel Panel (variance ↓). Boosting is Sequential Tutoring: each new tree studies the last one's mistakes (bias ↓).  Feature bagging is deliberately handicapping each tree, which sounds perverse. The point is in the covariance term: a tree forbidden from using the dominant feature at a split has to find a different question, so it makes different mistakes. Each tree is individually worse and the ensemble is better. The whole algorithm, in plain steps — for t = 1 … T: (1) draw a bootstrap sample of N rows with replacement; (2) grow a deep tree on it, but at every split only consider a random subset of max_features columns; (3) keep the tree. To predict: run the new point down all T trees and take the majority vote (or the average probability). No tree is pruned; the averaging does the job pruning would have done. interactive lab forest Start with 1 tree, then slide to 25 and compare the two panels: the single tree's jagged islands around noisy points versus the forest's smooth vote. Then switch both randomness options off — every tree becomes identical and the forest is no better than one tree. At the defaults, tree #1 alone scores 84.0% on the held-out points and the 25-tree forest 92.0%; with both switches off, every tree (and so the forest) scores 87.3%. Why voting works, with numbers: suppose each of 25 independent trees is right 65% of the time on some hard point. The majority (13 or more) is right whenever at least 13 of the 25 are right, which happens about 94% of the time — a binomial sum. Real trees are not independent, so the gain is smaller, and that is exactly why the forest works so hard (bootstrap rows, random features) to make them disagree. More trees never overfits a random forest — it only costs time. n_estimators is the one knob in this course that does not trade off against anything, which is why it does not appear in the complexity table in Module 7. tree, bagging, forest, compared import pandas as pd
from sklearn.tree import DecisionTreeClassifier
from sklearn.ensemble import BaggingClassifier, RandomForestClassifier
from sklearn.metrics import f1_score
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

def report(name, m):
    m.fit(X_train, y_train)
    tr, te = f1_score(y_train, m.predict(X_train)), f1_score(y_test, m.predict(X_test))
    print(f"{name:<28} train F1 {tr:.3f}  test F1 {te:.3f}  gap {tr - te:.3f}")
    return m

report("Tree (gini, unconstrained)", DecisionTreeClassifier(class_weight="balanced", random_state=42))
report("Tree (entropy)", DecisionTreeClassifier(criterion="entropy", class_weight="balanced", random_state=42))
report("Tree (max_depth=5)", DecisionTreeClassifier(max_depth=5, class_weight="balanced", random_state=42))
report("Bagging (200 trees)", BaggingClassifier(
    estimator=DecisionTreeClassifier(min_samples_split=10, class_weight="balanced"),
    n_estimators=200, max_samples=0.7, bootstrap=True, oob_score=True, random_state=42))
rf = report("Random forest", RandomForestClassifier(
    n_estimators=200, min_samples_split=10, class_weight="balanced",
    max_features="sqrt", random_state=42, n_jobs=-1))

imp = pd.Series(rf.feature_importances_, index=X_train.columns).nlargest(10)
imp.plot(kind="barh"); plt.title("Top 10 features"); plt.show() `max_features="sqrt"` is the feature bagging. Remove it and a RandomForestClassifier becomes plain bagging — which is a one-line experiment worth running. class_weight="balanced" inside a tree does something concrete to the split criterion. In an 8-stay / 2-churn node, the weights are 10/(2×8) = 0.625 and 10/(2×2) = 2.5, so the effective counts become 5 and 5 and the node's Gini rises from 0.32 to 0.50. The tree now has a reason to separate the churners.

This is the most instructive result in the whole assessment, and it looks like a bug the first time you see it. Models averaged Test MSE 1 0.5566 2 0.5569 3 0.5535 4 0.5538 2 → 30 (every even n) flat, 0.553–0.558 throughout Bagging over linear regression on California housing. Study guide Part 4, Q17–Q21. Why the curve is flat: the base learner is linear regression — a low-variance, stable model. Bootstrap resamples barely change its fitted line, so the thirty models are nearly identical. The covariance term in the variance formula is almost as large as the variance itself, so averaging cancels nothing. Bagging only reduces variance, and there was no variance to reduce. That flat curve is the correct answer, not a mistake in your code. Swap in a deep decision tree and the curve drops clearly, because a deep tree is exactly the unstable learner bagging was designed for. Be ready to say this in a viva. Assignment-1 Part 4 (Q16–Q21) graded details: write get_random_indices with rng.choice(n, size=n, replace=True) and the test set is never resampled. Average the predictions and then compute MSE once — that is different from averaging the individual MSEs, and the solution notebook prints both for Q21 to cover either reading. Each model and each loop iteration needs new random indices (the rubric says "new models trained" per iteration). Q21 loops range(2, 31, 2) and plots train and test MSE against n. Bagging a stable learner. As above — no variance, no benefit, and you have paid K times the compute. Reading feature importances as causes. They measure impurity reduction in this forest; correlated features split the credit arbitrarily, and a feature can look unimportant simply because a correlated twin absorbed the splits. Trusting OOB when the data is tiny. With few rows each tree's out-of-bag set is small and the estimate is noisy. Expecting a forest to extrapolate. Every leaf still predicts a mean, so a regression forest is still bounded by its training targets. Losing interpretability silently. A forest is 200 trees. If someone needs rules they can read, a shallow tree is the deliverable and the forest is the benchmark. ISLP Ch 8 ISLP chapter 8 covers bagging, random forests, out-of-bag error and boosting in sequence, with the same √p default for classification and the same explanation of why decorrelating the trees matters more than averaging more of them.

dataset churn Unconstrained tree: near-perfect train F1, weak test F1. High variance. Bagging (200 trees, 70% samples, min_samples_split=10): train F1 drops, test F1 rises, gap shrinks. Random forest: same idea plus decorrelated trees, usually the most stable. Note what happens to the training score: it falls. An ensemble is not a way to fit the training data better — it is a way to fit it less and generalise more. If your ensemble's training score goes up, something is wrong.

Reproduce Assignment Q16–Q21: write get_random_indices , train n models for n = 2, 4, …, 30, average the predictions, and plot train and test MSE against n. Success: a flat curve around 0.553–0.558, and you can explain why that is correct. Count the unique rows in one bootstrap sample of the training set. Success: about 63%, matching 10,449 / 16,512. Swap the base learner for DecisionTreeRegressor(max_depth=None) and redraw the curve. Success: it drops clearly, and you can say which term in the variance formula moved. On the churn data, run tree / bagging / forest and tabulate train F1, test F1 and the gap. Success: the gap shrinks left to right while test F1 rises. Set max_features=None on the forest to turn off feature bagging. Success: it performs like plain bagging, demonstrating what the decorrelation was buying. Stretch goals Verify the 36.8% rule empirically: for N = 10, 100, 1000, draw 2,000 bootstrap samples each and plot the average left-out fraction converging on 1/e. Compare the forest's oob_score_ with a proper 5-fold cross-validated score on the same data. They should be close — that closeness is why OOB is useful. Fit GradientBoostingClassifier on churn and compare its train/test gap with the forest's. Boosting should reduce bias and show a different failure mode. Go deeper: boosting and XGBoost (post-read preview) AdaBoost trains small trees (often stumps) one after another, increasing the weight of examples the previous tree got wrong. The final vote weights each tree by its accuracy. Gradient boosting fits each new tree to the residuals (errors) of the ensemble so far, a form of gradient descent in function space. A learning rate shrinks each tree's contribution. XGBoost / LightGBM are fast, regularised gradient-boosting libraries. On tabular business data (churn, credit risk, demand), they are usually the model to beat. Key knobs: n_estimators (more trees), learning_rate (smaller = slower but safer), max_depth (3–8 typical), subsample and colsample_bytree (bagging-style randomness). Unlike a random forest, boosting can overfit with too many trees, because each one is fitted to the previous ensemble's errors. n_estimators stops being a free knob the moment you switch from bagging to boosting.

Bagging is a Parallel Panel (variance ↓). Boosting is Sequential Tutoring (bias ↓). Averaging halves variance only when the models are uncorrelated — the covariance term is the whole story. (1 − 1/N)ᴺ → 1/e ≈ 0.368 left out, 63.2% in. Measured: 10,449 / 16,512. Feature bagging handicaps each tree so the ensemble disagrees more and cancels more. Bagging linear regression does nothing: there was no variance to reduce. The flat curve is correct. Why did bagging not improve linear regression? Linear regression is low-variance and stable, so bootstrap resamples barely change the fitted line and all the models are nearly identical. Bagging only reduces variance, and there was almost none. Test MSE stayed flat at 0.553–0.558 from 1 to 30 models. Why about 63% unique rows in a bootstrap sample? The chance a given row is never picked in N draws is (1 − 1/N)ᴺ, which tends to 1/e ≈ 0.368. So 63.2% are included — measured as 10,449 of 16,512. What does a random forest add to bagging, and why? Feature bagging — only a random subset of features (typically √p) is considered at each split. Bagged trees correlate when one feature dominates, and the covariance term then blocks the variance reduction; restricting features decorrelates them. Does adding more trees overfit a random forest? No — it only costs time. Boosting is different: each tree fits the previous ensemble's errors, so too many trees can overfit there.

Every model so far has been handed the right answers. K-means is the first one that is not — and most data in the world arrives without labels, because labelling is expensive and somebody has to do it by hand. Unsupervised learning = no labels; find structure. K-means partitions data into k clusters and is the simplest useful instance of it: no training signal, no accuracy to report, and an answer that depends on where you started. Customer segmentation is the canonical use: nobody labelled your customers as "price-sensitive" or "loyal", but the groups are latent in the behaviour. Also image colour quantisation, document grouping, and compressing a 1,536-dimensional embedding space into a few hundred representative centroids for faster retrieval. Assignment-1 Part 5 (Q22–Q28, 30 marks) requires this from scratch . The question says "from scratch" and the rubric explicitly checks for it — sklearn.cluster.KMeans is disallowed. This chapter is structured around the six functions it asks for.

docs.sectionTitle: Live: distance is the whole algorithm
docs.text: K-means is "nearest centroid" repeated, so everything it does is downstream of how you measure distance. Unscaled features mean the biggest-unit column decides every assignment — the same trap as k-NN, SVM and PCA. interactive lab vectors

Not scaling. A column in rupees and a column in counts means the rupees decide every cluster. Standardise first — this is the number-one K-means mistake. Picking k by minimising SSE. SSE is monotonically decreasing in k and reaches zero at k = n. Use the elbow, or a silhouette score. Expecting reproducibility without a seed. Different initialisation, different local minimum. Fix the seed and say so. Production code runs n_init restarts and keeps the best. Non-convex clusters. Two crescents or concentric rings cannot be separated by nearest-centroid regions, which are always convex. Use DBSCAN or spectral clustering instead. Very unequal cluster sizes. K-means tends to split a large cluster and merge small ones, because that lowers SSE. Reporting "accuracy". There are no labels. If you happen to have them, the cluster ids are arbitrary and must be matched to labels before any comparison means anything. Empty clusters. A centroid can lose every point. Without the guard in Q23 its mean is NaN and the run is ruined. ISLP Ch 12 ISLP chapter 12 presents K-means alongside hierarchical clustering, proves that the algorithm decreases the objective at every step, and makes the point that because it finds a local optimum you should run it several times from different random starts.

dataset cancer The breast-cancer data is a good honest test, because you have labels but the algorithm does not. Run K-means with k = 2 on the scaled features and then — only afterwards — check how well the two clusters line up with benign and malignant. If they line up well, the classes were separable in the feature geometry all along, which is consistent with what PCA showed in Module 2 and what the linear classifier achieved in Module 3. clustering without labels, then checking against them from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler
import numpy as np, pandas as pd

df = pd.read_csv("breast_cancer.csv", index_col=0).drop(columns="id")
y = (df["diagnosis"] == "M").to_numpy()
X = StandardScaler().fit_transform(df.drop(columns="diagnosis"))   # scale FIRST

c0 = initialize_centroids(42, 2, X)
centroids, clusters = kmeans(2, X, c0)
print("SSE:", round(compute_sse(centroids, clusters, 2), 1))

labels = np.array([closest_centroid(x, centroids) for x in X])
# Cluster ids are arbitrary, so align them with the labels before comparing
agree = max((labels == y).mean(), (labels != y).mean())
print("agreement with diagnosis:", round(agree, 3))
print(pd.crosstab(labels, y, rownames=["cluster"], colnames=["malignant"])) The `max` of the two agreements is the alignment step: cluster 0 might correspond to malignant or to benign, and nothing in the algorithm decides which.

This is Assignment-1 Part 5, worth 30 marks. Write all six functions yourself; do not import KMeans . Write closest_centroid , compute_centroids , initialize_centroids , compute_sse and kmeans . Success: all five match the signatures in the table, with the empty-cluster guard and the np.allclose stop. Loop k = 1 to 4 with seed 42 using your kmeans , and print every SSE. Success: 492.6, 86.3, 41.0, 27.5. Plot SSE against k and identify the elbow. Success: k = 2, and you can justify it from the drop column rather than the SSE column. Run k = 2 and scatter the clusters in two colours with the centroids as red X markers. Success: two visibly separated groups and two marked centroids. Confirm replace=False matters by running with replace=True a few times. Success: you can produce a run where two centroids start on the same point. Stretch goals Run your K-means from ten different seeds and record the final SSE for each. The spread is the local-minimum problem, measured — and it is why sklearn defaults to n_init=10 . Cluster the breast-cancer data with k = 2 and compare against the real diagnoses, remembering to align the arbitrary cluster ids first. Implement k-means++ initialisation — choose each new centroid with probability proportional to its squared distance from the nearest existing one — and show it reaches a lower SSE more often than uniform random starts. Build make_moons data and watch K-means fail on it. Then say in one sentence why, using the word convex .

Initialise, assign to nearest, update to the mean, repeat until nothing moves. Each step is optimal given the other, which is why it converges — to a local minimum. SSE always falls, so only the bend in the curve tells you k. Ours bends hard at 2: 492.6 → 86.3 → 41.0 → 27.5. Nearest-centroid regions are convex, so crescents and rings defeat it. Scale first, seed it, guard against empty clusters, and stop on a tolerance not on equality. Why can K-means give different answers on different runs? Random initialisation. The algorithm converges to a local minimum of SSE, and which one depends on where the centroids started — hence the fixed seed, and hence n_init restarts in production. Why is SSE alone a bad way to choose k? It decreases monotonically with k and reaches zero when every point is its own cluster, so minimising it always picks k = n. You look for the elbow instead. What are the four steps of the algorithm? Initialise k centroids; assign every point to its nearest centroid; move each centroid to the mean of its assigned points; repeat until the centroids stop moving within a tolerance. Why does an empty cluster need special handling? Its mean is the mean of nothing, which is NaN, and that NaN then propagates through every subsequent distance. The fix is to keep the old centroid for that cluster. Why does K-means fail on two interleaved crescents? A cluster is defined as the set of points nearest one centroid, and that region is always convex. A crescent is not convex, so no set of centroids can carve it out.

docs.sectionTitle: Why the order is the content
docs.text: Use this page the night before an exam or an interview. Every line points back to a module. You now know nine or ten algorithms. The thing that separates somebody who can use them from somebody who has read about them is not knowing another one — it is running the same nine steps in the same order, every time, without skipping the boring ones. Most of the ways a project goes wrong are ordering mistakes, not modelling mistakes.

Frame : classification or regression? What mistake is costlier (FP or FN)? That fixes the metric. Load and inspect : shape, dtypes, info, describe, head. Fix numbers-stored-as-text. EDA : duplicates, missing values, class balance, histograms (skew), box plots (outliers), correlation heatmap. Split (stratified for classification). From here on, the test set is sealed. Preprocess on train only : impute, cap or impute outliers, encode categories (one-hot), scale (for linear models, SVM, PCA, k-NN; trees don't need it), drop redundant features. Baseline : majority class or a simple linear / logistic model. Model + tune with cross-validation inside a Pipeline. Evaluate once on test: the right metric, the train/test gap, the confusion matrix. Threshold and explain : choose the operating point; feature importance or coefficients. "Fresh Lemons Excite Sour People But Make Excellent Tea" Frame, Load, EDA, Split, Preprocess, Baseline, Model, Evaluate, Threshold. Why each step sits where it does Frame first, because the metric decides what "better" means. If you choose the metric after seeing results you will choose the one that flatters them. Deciding that a missed tumour is worse than a false alarm takes one sentence and must happen before any code. Split fourth, before any statistic is computed. Every preprocessing step in step 5 — medians, fences, means, standard deviations, correlation matrices, PCA components, encodings — is learnt from data. Learn any of them from all the rows and the test set has influenced your model. This is the single rule that matters most, and Module 3 made it a graded point. Baseline sixth, before anything complicated. It costs two minutes and tells you the floor. On churn the majority baseline is 73% accurate — knowing that before you build an SVM is what stops you from celebrating 75%. Evaluate once, eighth. The test set is a measuring instrument and it is consumed by use. Every time you look at it and change something in response, the number it gives you drifts further from the truth. Threshold last, ninth. The operating point is a business decision made on validation data, and it is separable from fitting the model. Doing it last means you can change it later without retraining. Step Where it was taught The mistake it prevents Frame Grading a classifier (M3) Choosing the metric that flatters the result Load & inspect Pandas tables (M0) Modelling a column that is secretly text EDA Plotting (M0), Describing data (M1) Assuming a shape the data does not have Split The cancer pipeline (M3) Leakage — the big one Preprocess on train only Data challenges (M3) Leakage through a median or a scaler Baseline Class imbalance (M5) Celebrating a score the majority class already gets Model + tune in a Pipeline Model complexity (M3), Imbalance (M5) Leakage inside the cross-validation fold Evaluate once Model complexity (M3) Tuning on test Threshold & explain Logistic regression (M4) Shipping 0.5 because it was the default

Skipping Frame. The commonest and the most expensive. You get a model that optimises accuracy on a problem where accuracy is meaningless. Skipping Baseline. You have no idea whether your model is good, only what number it produced. Splitting late. Everything downstream is contaminated and nothing warns you — the score just comes out a little too high. Preprocessing outside the Pipeline. Cross-validated scores become optimistic by an amount you cannot estimate. Evaluating on test repeatedly. Each look spends a little of the test set's value. Stopping at step 8. A model with no chosen operating point is not deployable; somebody downstream will pick 0.5 for you. Trees do not need scaling; linear models, SVMs, PCA, k-NN and K-means all do. Putting a scaler in front of a random forest is harmless but tells a reviewer you were following a recipe rather than thinking. Leaving it out of an SVM is a real bug. ISLP Ch 5 ISLP chapter 5 is the authority on step 7 — why cross-validation inside the training set is the right way to choose between models, and what goes wrong when the selection step sees the data it is later validated on.

It takes ten minutes and saves a day. dataset churn

Run all nine steps end to end on a dataset you have not used yet in this course — the student survey, predicting passed . Frame it in writing before any code: classification, which error is worse, which metric. Success: three sentences, committed to before you look at a score. Load, inspect and do EDA. Success: you can state the class balance and name the most skewed column. Split stratified, then build everything else inside a Pipeline . Success: no statistic is computed outside the fold. Establish the majority baseline. Success: you have a number to beat before you fit anything. Fit logistic regression and a random forest, tuned by cross-validation. Success: you report cross-validated scores, not test scores, for the comparison. Evaluate the winner on test exactly once, then choose a threshold on validation and justify it. Success: one test number, one defended operating point. Stretch goals Deliberately break step 4: scale and impute before splitting, run the whole thing, and compare the test score with the honest version. The difference is what leakage buys you, and it is why reviewers look for it. Write the nine steps as a reusable function skeleton with the dataset-specific parts as arguments. Then run it on two course datasets without editing the body.

Fresh Lemons Excite Sour People But Make Excellent Tea. Frame first: the metric comes from the cost of the mistake, decided before any code. Split fourth: every statistic afterwards is learnt from train only. Baseline sixth: know the floor before you celebrate a number. Evaluate once: the test set is a measuring instrument consumed by use. Name the nine steps in order. Frame, Load and inspect, EDA, Split, Preprocess on train only, Baseline, Model and tune with cross-validation, Evaluate once on test, Threshold and explain. Why does the split come before preprocessing? Imputation values, outlier fences, scaler statistics, correlation matrices and PCA components are all learnt from data. Learning them from all rows lets the test set influence the model, which is leakage. Why bother with a baseline? It tells you the floor. On churn, 'nobody leaves' is 73% accurate, so a 75% model is almost worthless — and you cannot know that without the baseline. Which models in this course do not need scaling? Decision trees and their ensembles. Linear and logistic regression with a penalty, SVMs, PCA, k-NN and K-means all do.

docs.chapterTitle: Which model when, which metric when, which way each knob turns
docs.sectionTitle: Why three tables and not a flowchart
docs.text: There is no decision tree for choosing a model, and anyone who gives you one has hidden the judgement rather than removed it. What there is: a handful of properties worth checking (how many rows, how many features, is the boundary curved, does a human need to read the result, what does a mistake cost) and a reliable sense of which knob moves complexity in which direction. These three tables are that sense, written down. They are the densest page in the portal and the one to read the night before anything.

docs.chapterTitle: Which model when, which metric when, which way each knob turns
docs.text: Model Reach for it when Avoid when Needs scaling? Linear regression Numeric target, roughly linear, need interpretability Strong curves, many outliers For regularised versions Ridge / Lasso Many features, overfitting; Lasso to select features Few features, no overfitting Yes Logistic regression Binary classification baseline, probabilities, explainable coefficients Complex non-linear boundaries (without feature engineering) Yes Linear SVM High-dimensional data (text), clear margin Need calibrated probabilities Yes RBF SVM Medium-sized data with curved boundaries Hundreds of thousands of rows (slow) Yes, essential Decision tree Need rules a manager can read; mixed feature types Need stable accuracy (high variance) No Random forest Strong tabular default with little tuning Need a tiny, fast, explainable model No Gradient boosting / XGBoost Best accuracy on tabular data Very small or noisy data without tuning No PCA (preprocessing) Too many correlated features, visualise in 2D, compress embeddings Need to keep named features Yes, essential  A shorter version for when you are under time pressure: start with logistic regression or linear regression , because it is fast, interpretable and tells you the floor. Then try a random forest , because it is the strongest thing you can get with almost no tuning. If the forest barely beats the linear model, the relationship is close to linear and you should keep the linear model. If it beats it by a lot, there is structure worth pursuing with boosting.

docs.chapterTitle: Which model when, which metric when, which way each knob turns
docs.sectionTitle: Which metric when, and which way each knob turns
docs.text: Situation Metric Balanced classes, mistakes cost the same Accuracy Missing a positive is costly (disease, fraud, churn, missile) Recall False alarms are costly (spam, unnecessary surgery, legal flags) Precision Imbalanced, both matter F1 (or PR-AUC) Regression, big errors very bad MSE / RMSE Regression, robust to outliers MAE  Which way does each knob turn complexity? Knob More complex (risk overfit) when… Polynomial degree higher Ridge / Lasso α lower C (logistic, SVM) higher RBF γ higher Tree max_depth higher min_samples_split / min_samples_leaf lower Number of PCA components higher Random forest n_estimators (more trees doesn't overfit; it just costs time) Learning rate (GD, boosting) (too high diverges; too low is slow)  α and C point opposite ways. α is the penalty; C is the patience for data.  The two parenthesised rows are the exceptions worth knowing, because they are the ones people get wrong in interviews. n_estimators in a bagging ensemble is free — more trees never overfits, it only costs time. In a boosting ensemble it is not free, because each tree fits the previous ensemble's errors. And the learning rate does not trade complexity at all: it trades convergence against stability. Diagnose from the train / test gap Train score Test score Diagnosis Do Low Low Underfitting (high bias) More features, more complex model, less regularisation High Much lower Overfitting (high variance) More data, regularise, simpler model, bagging, feature selection High Close to train Good fit Tune threshold, ship  Put the three tables together and you have a loop: read the gap, decide bias or variance, then look up which knob moves in which direction and turn it. That loop is most of practical machine learning. A small gap is not a good model. Ridge at α = 10⁴ on the breast-cancer data had a gap of 0.1 points and was eight points worse than plain linear regression. You need a small gap and a high level — row 3 of the diagnosis table, not just row 3's second column.

docs.chapterTitle: Which model when, which metric when, which way each knob turns
docs.text: Start linear, then random forest. If the forest barely wins, keep the linear model. The metric comes from the cost of the mistake, not from the data. α and C point opposite ways; n_estimators is free for bagging and not for boosting. Read the gap, decide bias or variance, then turn the matching knob. A small gap is not a good model — you need a small gap and a high level. Which way does complexity move for α, C, γ and max_depth? Complexity rises as α falls, as C rises, as γ rises and as max_depth rises. α is a penalty; C is the inverse of one. Which metric for an imbalanced problem where both error types matter? F1, or PR-AUC if you want it across all thresholds. Accuracy is misleading and precision or recall alone is gameable. Does adding trees to a random forest risk overfitting? No — it only costs time. Boosting is the opposite: each tree fits the ensemble's remaining errors, so too many trees can overfit. Train and test are both 90% and close together. Good model? Not necessarily. A small gap means low variance, not a good model — Ridge at α=10⁴ had a 0.1-point gap and was eight points worse than a plain linear fit. You need the level as well as the gap.

docs.chapterTitle: How Module 1 powers Gen AI, and the formula sheet
docs.sectionTitle: Why none of this is a detour
docs.text: It is easy to read Module 1 as the boring prerequisite before the interesting part — the classical statistics you have to get through before you reach language models and agents. It is not. A transformer is dot products, softmax and cross-entropy, trained by gradient descent with weight decay. A RAG retriever is cosine similarity over embeddings. Self-consistency is ensemble voting. Fine-tuning on a small dataset is overfitting, and holding out an eval set is the fix. There is no second body of mathematics waiting after this one — there is this one, at scale.

docs.chapterTitle: How Module 1 powers Gen AI, and the formula sheet
docs.text: Module 1 idea Inside a Gen AI / agentic system Vectors, embeddings Every token, document and user is a vector Cosine similarity RAG retrieval, semantic search, picking which tool an agent should call Dot product, ÷ scale Attention: query·key, divided by √d to keep numbers stable Vector addition Residual stream, token + position embeddings Softmax + cross-entropy Next-token prediction training Gradient descent, learning rate Pre-training and fine-tuning L2 regularisation Weight decay Temperature (scaling scores) Logits ÷ T before sampling: low T sharper, high T more random PCA / dimensionality reduction Compressing embeddings for vector stores Ensembles and voting Self-consistency (sample several answers, majority vote), model routing Class imbalance, precision/recall Evaluating guardrails, rare-incident detection, hallucination flags Bias–variance, overfitting Fine-tuning on tiny datasets memorises; hold out an eval set  Three worth following through properly Attention is a dot product with a scale. A token's query vector is dotted with every other token's key vector, giving one similarity score per pair — exactly the weighted-score reading from Module 2. The division by √d is there because the dot product of two d-dimensional vectors grows with d, and without the division the scores would be large enough to saturate the softmax. That is the "scale" operation from the vectors chapter, used to keep numbers in a workable range. Next-token prediction is the digit reader. The output is a one-hot target over a vocabulary instead of over ten digits, the loss is cross-entropy, and the training is gradient descent. Same four-step recipe from Module 3, with 100,000 classes instead of 10. Temperature is the threshold decision again. Dividing logits by T before sampling makes the distribution sharper (low T) or flatter (high T), which trades confident-but-narrow against varied-but-risky. Structurally it is the same choice as moving a classifier's threshold: the model has not changed, only the operating point. Which means the diagnostic habits transfer too. A fine-tune that memorises a 200-example dataset is high variance and shows the same train/eval gap you watched at polynomial degree 3. A retrieval system that returns plausible-but-wrong documents has a precision problem, and lowering the similarity cut-off trades precision for recall exactly as the threshold lab shows.

docs.chapterTitle: How Module 1 powers Gen AI, and the formula sheet
docs.text: Knowing the edges of what you have learnt is as useful as knowing the middle. None of the following appeared here, and each is a real gap rather than a detail: Neural networks beyond one neuron. Stacking layers, activation functions, backpropagation through them. The single neuron and gradient descent are the ingredients; the assembly is a later module. Boosting in depth. AdaBoost and gradient boosting got a preview in Module 6, not a treatment — and on tabular data they are usually the model to beat. Time series. Everything here assumes rows are exchangeable. They are not when they are ordered in time, and a random split is actively wrong there. Causal inference. Every coefficient in this module is an association. Nothing here licenses a causal claim. Calibration and uncertainty. Logistic regression gives a probability; whether that probability is trustworthy is a separate question with its own tooling. Deployment. Drift, monitoring, retraining cadence — the part where a model meets the world and slowly stops working.

docs.chapterTitle: How Module 1 powers Gen AI, and the formula sheet
docs.text: Cover the right column of the Gen AI table and reconstruct it from the left. Success: at least ten of the twelve, and you can explain the √d division without looking. Write out the formula sheet from memory, group by group. Success: you can produce Bayes, the SVM objective, IG and the out-of-bag probability unaided. Implement scaled dot-product attention for three toy token vectors: dot every query with every key, divide by √d, softmax, and use the weights to average the values. Success: the weights sum to 1 per row and the most similar token gets the most weight. For each of the six gaps above, name which later module or external resource would close it. Success: you have a reading plan rather than a feeling of incompleteness. Stretch goals Build a minimal RAG retriever end to end: embed five documents with any sentence-transformer, embed a query, rank by cosine, pick a cut-off and justify it. Every step is a Module 1 or Module 2 idea. Demonstrate temperature: take a vector of logits, divide by T for T = 0.2, 1 and 5, softmax each, and plot the three distributions. Then say which one you would ship and for what. Fine-tune anything on 50 examples and plot train versus eval loss. You will reproduce polynomial degree 3, in a different costume.

docs.chapterTitle: How Module 1 powers Gen AI, and the formula sheet
docs.text: Attention is a dot product divided by √d to keep the softmax from saturating. Next-token prediction is the digit reader with 100,000 classes. Temperature is the decision threshold, moved at sampling time. Self-consistency is ensemble voting; weight decay is L2. A fine-tune on 200 examples is high variance, and a held-out eval set is the fix. Why is attention divided by √d? The dot product of two d-dimensional vectors grows with d, so without the division the scores become large enough to saturate the softmax into a near-one-hot distribution with vanishing gradients. It is the scale operation from vector arithmetic. Which Module 1 idea is RAG retrieval? Cosine similarity over embeddings — the query and every document become vectors, and the top matches by angle are retrieved. Where you put the cut-off is a precision/recall trade, not a mathematical fact. What loss trains a GPT-style model? Cross-entropy on next-token prediction — the same loss as the handwritten-digit classifier, over a vocabulary instead of ten digits. A fine-tune on 200 examples scores well on training and badly on held-out data. What is that? High variance — overfitting. The same diagnosis as a degree-3 polynomial on 455 rows, and the same fixes: more data, less capacity, stronger regularisation, and an honest eval set.

docs.sectionTitle: Why marks go missing on correct answers
docs.text: Most lost marks are not wrong answers. They are right answers that skipped a specific thing the rubric asked for. The rubric checks for particular arguments, particular printed output and particular implementations — not just the final number. A K-means solution that uses sklearn.cluster.KMeans is correct and scores nothing. An SVM fitted without loss='hinge' gives a plausible margin and the wrong one. This page is every such detail from the five parts, in one list, so you can run it as a pre-submission check.

Part 1 — Linear regression (Q1–Q5, 10 marks) Q2 inverts the usual direction on purpose : input is MedHouseVal , target is MedInc . Follow it exactly — the rubric checks this. Print both shapes: X = df[['MedHouseVal']] → (20640, 1) and y = df['MedInc'] → (20640,). The shape convention is the trap underneath it: sklearn wants X as 2D (n_samples, n_features) and y as 1D (n_samples,) . df['col'] is 1D; df[['col']] is 2D. Q3 wants a scatter with small transparent dots ( s=5, alpha=0.3 ) because there are 20,640 points, and Q5 wants the fitted line drawn over that scatter in a distinguishable colour. Q Expected Value Q4 reg.coef_[0] 1.1328 Q4 reg.intercept_ 1.5274  Part 2 — Logistic regression (Q6–Q10, 10 marks) Q8: LabelEncoder maps classes alphabetically — setosa 0, versicolor 1, virginica 2. So drop versicolor with data[data.Species != 1] and relabel virginica with .replace(2, 1) , leaving 50 of class 0 and 50 of class 1. Q9: train_test_split(x, y, test_size=0.2, random_state=42) → train (80, 4), test (20, 4). Q10 wants the weights and the bias printed , not only the accuracy. Q Expected Value Q10 coef_ [0.46, −0.31, 1.73, 0.81] Q10 intercept_ −8.35 Q10 accuracy_score 1.0  Part 3 — Support vector classifier (Q11–Q15, 20 marks) LinearSVC defaults to squared hinge, so loss='hinge' must be passed explicitly — this is rubric-checked. Add max_iter=100000 to avoid convergence warnings at C=1000. The 7-mark questions want the boundary and both margins drawn over the whole dataset: solve w₀x₀ + w₁x₁ + b = c for x₁, giving x₁ = −(w₀x₀ + b − c) / w₁ with c = 0, +1, −1. Take w = svc.coef_[0] and b = svc.intercept_[0] . Q Setting Margin width Q14 C = 1 0.639 Q15 C = 1000 0.243 Test accuracy is 1.0 in both cases — this data is easy, so only the margin moves. Part 4 — Bagging (Q16–Q21, 30 marks) Three separate traps. (a) Average the predictions and then compute MSE once — that is not the same as averaging the individual MSEs, and the solution notebook prints both for Q21 to cover either reading of "average mean squared error". (b) Each model and each loop iteration needs new random indices — the rubric says "new models trained" per iteration. (c) The test set is never resampled : bootstrap only the training rows. the three lines the rubric is looking for def get_random_indices(n, rng):
    return rng.choice(n, size=n, replace=True)     # with replacement

idx = get_random_indices(len(x_train), rng)
x_var, y_var = x_train[idx], y_train[idx]          # training variation only

The lecture's formulation and the rubric both want plain hinge. Why is averaging the MSEs different from the MSE of the averaged predictions? Squaring is not linear, so the mean of squared errors is not the squared error of the mean. Bagging averages the predictions first and then scores once — that is where the variance reduction appears.
